title: Elements of Sampling Survey
text:
Preface
Statistical inference in the real world almost always deals with bounded, finite populations—whether we are estimating agricultural yields, public health metrics, or economic indicators. This book explores the mathematical theory and practical mechanics of drawing reliable samples from those populations, examining how intelligent survey design directly dictates the precision and cost of our conclusions. The chapters cover a comprehensive suite of methodologies, including simple random sampling, stratified random sampling, cluster and systematic sampling, probability proportionate to size (PPS) sampling, and powerful auxiliary-variable strategies like difference, ratio, and regression estimation.
This book is part of the course materials for STAT 348 Sampling Techniques, which also has the slides, the Shinylive apps and the syllabus.
Key Features

Custom R Functions: Rather than relying exclusively on pre-built packages, this text emphasizes writing custom functions to analyze survey data, helping students learn how R works under the hood.
Modern R Workflows: Data manipulation and presentation leverage the modern R ecosystem, utilizing dplyr for clean wrangling, ggplot2 for advanced visualization, and gt for publication-ready mathematical tables.
Simulation-Based Learning: Extensive simulation studies demonstrate the practical differences between sampling schemes, with a core focus on how predictive auxiliary variables improve precision and reduce variance.

title: 1  Introduction to Sampling Survey
text:
1.1 A Bad Sampling Example
A sample survey collects information about a population by measuring only part of it. This chapter introduces the main ideas. We start with a survey that went badly wrong, then define the basic terms, describe the errors that can spoil a survey, and sketch the main designs studied in the rest of the book. The second half sets up the framework of probability sampling that all later chapters use: samples and their probabilities, inclusion probabilities and sampling weights, population quantities, sampling distributions, and bias, variance and mean squared error. The material corresponds to Chapter 1 and Section 2.2 of Lohr, and Chapters 2 and 3.1–3.4 of Scheaffer et al.
Shere Hite’s book Women and Love: A Cultural Revolution in Progress (1987) reported a number of widely quoted results:
The book was widely criticized in newspaper and magazine articles throughout the United States. The Time magazine cover story “Back Off, Buddy” (October 12, 1987) called the conclusions of the study “dubious” and “of limited value”. The problem was not the arithmetic but the way the data were collected:
A large number of responses (4,500) did not make up for any of these problems. The rest of this chapter names the problems precisely, and the rest of the book shows how a properly designed probability sample avoids the first two.

title: 1  Introduction to Sampling Survey
1  Introduction to Sampling Survey
text:
1.2 Elements of Sampling Problems

1.2.1 Basic definitions

Observation unit. An object on which a measurement is taken; also called an element. In studies of human populations, the observation units are often individuals.
Target population. The complete collection of observations we want to study. Defining the target population is often harder than it seems. Should a political poll target all adults eligible to vote, all registered voters, or everyone who voted in the last election?
Sample. A subset of a population.
Sampled population. The collection of all possible observation units that might have been chosen in the sample: the population from which the sample was actually taken.
Sampling unit. A unit that can be selected for a sample. We may want to study individuals but have no list of them. Instead we select households, which are then the sampling units, while the individuals remain the observation units.
Sampling frame. A list, map or other specification of the sampling units from which the sample may be selected, for example a list of telephone numbers, street addresses or farms.



1.2.2 Target and sampled populations
In an ideal survey the sampled population equals the target population. This ideal is rarely met (Figure 1.1). Some members of the target population are not in the sampling frame. Some who are in the frame cannot be reached, refuse to respond, or are not capable of responding. And the frame may contain units that are not eligible for the survey at all.






Figure 1.1: Target population, sampling frame population and sampled population. The sampled population is only the part of the target population that is in the frame and can and will respond.



In the Hite study the element was an individual woman and the target population was all adult U.S. women. The sampled population, however, was women who belonged to the organizations that received questionnaires and who would complete and return them.

title: 1  Introduction to Sampling Survey
text:
1.3 Selection Bias
Selection bias occurs when part of the target population is not in the sampled population or, more generally, when some population units are sampled at a different rate than intended by the investigator. A sample of convenience is often biased, because the units that are easiest to select, or most likely to respond, are usually not representative of the harder-to-select or nonresponding units. For example:

A convenience sample of adolescents used to study communication about AIDS probably overestimated how much parents and teenagers talk about it. Adolescents willing to talk to investigators are also more likely to talk to other authority figures, such as their parents.
Misspecifying the target population. Polls before the 1994 Arizona gubernatorial primary predicted that Eddie Basha would trail by 9 or more points; he won with 37% of the vote. The polls targeted people who had voted in past primaries and missed the new rural voters who supported Basha.

Selection bias has several common sources.
Undercoverage is the failure to include all of the target population in the sampling frame. The U.S. Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, a telephone survey, misses households without telephones and for many years missed households with only cell phones. Coverage varies by region and by income, so undercoverage can bias the estimates.
Overcoverage is the inclusion in the sampling frame of units that are not in the target population, for example when interviewers include respondents under 18 in a radio survey meant for adults only.
Nonresponse is the failure to obtain responses from all of the units chosen for the sample. It distorts the results even when the other sources of selection bias are minimized. Nonrespondents often differ in critical ways from respondents, but the extent of the difference is usually unknown. Some published surveys have response rates as low as 10%. It is difficult to generalize from such a survey when 90% of the sample could not be reached or refused to take part.

title: 1  Introduction to Sampling Survey
text:
1.4 Measurement Error
When a response differs from the true value, measurement error has occurred. Measurement bias occurs when the responses tend to differ from the truth in one direction. Like selection bias, measurement bias must be considered and minimized at the design stage; no amount of data analysis can remove it afterwards. Some sources of measurement error:

People do not always tell the truth. Farmers receiving food aid may underreport their crop yields, hoping to receive more aid.
People do not always understand the questions. A 1993 Roper poll found that 25% of Americans did not believe the Holocaust had happened. The question used a confusing double negative. When it was reworded, only 1% thought it “possible” that the Holocaust never happened.
People forget. In the U.S. National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS), respondents asked about crimes in the last six months sometimes include events from further back. This is called telescoping.

Careful questionnaire design reduces measurement error:

Always test the questions on a small group before the survey is carried out.
Keep the questions simple and clear. Belson (1981) tested the question “What proportion of your evening viewing time do you spend watching news programmes?” on 53 people. Only 14 interpreted “proportion” correctly, as a percentage, part or fraction.
Use specific questions instead of general ones. Instead of asking “Did anyone attack you in the last six months?”, the NCVS asks a detailed series of questions: “With any weapon, for instance a gun or knife”, “With anything like a baseball bat, frying pan, scissors, or stick”, and so on.

title: 1  Introduction to Sampling Survey
text:
1.5 Sampling and Nonsampling Errors
Sampling error results from taking one sample instead of examining the whole population. A different sample would likely give a different result. Sampling error is what a poll’s “margin of error” describes, and because it comes from the random selection of the sample, it can be quantified in probabilistic terms. Most of this book is about measuring and reducing it.
Nonsampling errors, such as selection bias and measurement error, cannot be attributed to sample-to-sample variability. They are often far larger than the sampling error. A survey may proudly report a margin of error of 3% based on a 30% response rate, while ignoring the large selection bias that such a response rate may cause.

1.5.1 Why sample at all?
If samples have errors, why not always take a census of the whole population?

Cost. A sample provides reliable information at far less cost than a census, and with a probability sample the sampling error can be quantified. Some measurements are destructive (for example, pulverizing a cookie to measure its fat content), so a census is not even possible.
Speed. Data from a sample can be collected and processed more quickly, so the estimates are timely. An unemployment rate for 2005 published in 2015 would be useless.
Accuracy. Estimates from a sample can be more accurate than those from a census. A census requires a large administrative effort with many data collectors, while a smaller operation allows the investigators to be more careful and to reduce nonsampling errors.

section: 1.6 Overview of Probability Sampling and Estimation Techniques
text:
1.6 Overview of Probability Sampling and Estimation Techniques
In a probability sample, every unit in the population has a known, positive chance of being selected, and the sample is chosen by a random mechanism. This removes selection bias due to the investigator’s choices, and it makes it possible to quantify the sampling error. This section previews the techniques studied in the rest of the book: three basic designs for drawing the sample (simple random, stratified and cluster sampling), estimators that use auxiliary information (ratio and regression estimation), and designs with unequal selection probabilities. Each has its own chapter later in the book.
To compare the designs we use synthetic populations of \(N = 1000\) units, with the \(y\)-values drawn from exponential distributions. The population for SRS and stratified sampling (Figure 1.2 and Figure 1.3) consists of four strata of sizes 400, 300, 200 and 100 whose means differ a lot: each is an exponential distribution with mean 1.5, shifted by 0, 4, 8 and 12 respectively. The population for cluster sampling (Figure 1.4) consists of ten clusters whose sizes range from 40 to 160 units, exponential with means from 2 to 8. Each design selects \(n = 60\) units, shown in red; the unselected units are grey.
Simple random sampling. A simple random sample (SRS) is the simplest probability sample. An SRS of size \(n\) is taken when every possible subset of \(n\) units in the population has the same chance of being the sample. The design uses no information about the groups: in Figure 1.2 the 1000 units are listed in an arbitrary order, and 60 of them are chosen at random. By chance, a group may be over- or under-represented, and the sample values range over the whole spread of the population.








Figure 1.2: A simple random sample of \(n = 60\) (red) from a population of \(N = 1000\) units, listed in an arbitrary order. The dashed line is the population mean.





Stratified random sampling. In a stratified random sample, the population is divided into subgroups called strata, and an SRS is selected independently from each stratum. Strata are often subgroups of interest, such as provinces, terrain types or firm sizes. In Figure 1.3 the same 1000 units are arranged by stratum, with the strata sorted by their means (dashed lines). The sample is allocated in proportion to the stratum sizes, \(60 \times N_h/1000\), so 24, 18, 12 and 6 units are drawn from the four strata. Every stratum is represented in the sample in a fixed proportion. Stratification often increases precision, because units within a stratum tend to be more similar than units selected at random from the whole population. Here the stratum means are far apart while the spread within each stratum is small, so the differences between the strata, which make up most of the variation in Figure 1.2, no longer contribute to the sampling error.








Figure 1.3: A stratified random sample from the same population: the four strata are sorted by their means (dashed lines), and SRSs of 24, 18, 12 and 6 units (red) are drawn from the strata of sizes 400, 300, 200 and 100.





Cluster sampling. In a cluster sample, the observation units are grouped into larger sampling units called clusters. For example, to survey Lutheran church members in Minneapolis without a list of all members, we could take an SRS of churches (the clusters) and then subsample members within each selected church (the observation units). In Figure 1.4 the population consists of ten clusters of different sizes, from 40 to 160 units, sorted by their means. Three clusters are selected at random (shaded), and 20 units are subsampled in each. This is convenient, since only three clusters need to be visited, but the seven clusters that are not selected contribute nothing to the sample. When the cluster means differ, the estimate depends heavily on which clusters happen to be chosen. Members of the same church may likewise be more similar to each other than a random sample of Lutherans would be. A cluster sample therefore often provides less information than an SRS of the same size, and the gain in convenience must be weighed against the loss in precision.








Figure 1.4: A cluster sample from a population of ten clusters of 40 to 160 units, sorted by their means (dashed lines). Three clusters are selected at random (shaded), and 20 units (red) are subsampled in each; the other clusters are not observed at all.





Using auxiliary information: ratio and regression estimation. Often we know, for every unit in the population, an auxiliary variable \(x_i\) that is related to \(y_i\): last year’s value of \(y\), the size of a farm, the floor area of a store. Ratio and regression estimation take an ordinary sample but use the known \(x_i\) at the estimation stage. In Figure 1.5, \(y\) is roughly proportional to \(x\). From an SRS (green circles) we estimate the slope \(\hat B = \bar y/\bar x\) of the line \(y = Bx\) (red), and use it to predict \(y\) for every unit of the population from its known \(x_i\) (red points). The ratio estimate \(\hat{\bar y}_r = \hat B\,\bar x_U\) is the average of these predictions. In this sample the green units happen to have large \(x\), so the sample mean \(\bar y\) is too high. The ratio estimate corrects for this through the known \(\bar x_U\) and lands close to \(\bar y_U\). Regression estimation does the same with a fitted line \(y = B_0 + B_1x\) that need not pass through the origin. Both are studied in Section 5.1 and the sections that follow.








Figure 1.5: Ratio estimation. Grey: the population, whose \(x_i\) are all known. Green circles: an SRS. Red: the line \(y = \hat B x\) fitted from the sample and the predicted value \(\hat B x_i\) of every unit. Left margin: the population mean \(\bar y_U\) (black), the sample mean \(\bar y\) (green) and the ratio estimate \(\hat{\bar y}_r\), the mean of the red points.





Unequal probability sampling. Auxiliary information can also be used at the design stage. In unequal probability sampling (UPS), units are selected with different probabilities, usually proportional to a measure of size \(x_i\) that is expected to be roughly proportional to \(y_i\). Large units, which contribute most to the population total, are then more likely to be in the sample. In Figure 1.6 the units of Figure 1.2 are drawn again, each with a size measure \(x_i\) equal to \(y_i\) multiplied by a random error, and the point sizes show the inclusion probabilities \(\pi_i \propto x_i\). A sample of 60 units (red) is drawn with these probabilities. Most of the sampled units have large \(y\), so the plain sample mean would be far too high. Each unit must instead be weighted by its sampling weight \(w_i = 1/\pi_i\) (Section 1.7), which gives the many small units their due. When \(x_i\) is nearly proportional to \(y_i\), the weighted estimator \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} y_i/\pi_i\) of the total is very precise, because \(y_i/\pi_i\) is nearly the same for every unit. UPS is studied in Section 7.2 and the sections that follow.








Figure 1.6: Unequal probability sampling from the population of Figure 1.2. Each unit’s inclusion probability is proportional to a size measure \(x_i\) equal to \(y_i\) times a random error; point sizes show the probabilities. The \(n = 60\) sampled units (red) are mostly large ones. The dashed line is the population mean.

title: 1  Introduction to Sampling Survey
text:
1.7 A Framework for Probability Sampling
We now make the idea of a probability sample precise. The key concepts are the population, the sample, the probabilities of the samples, the inclusion probabilities, and the bias, variance and mean squared error of an estimator.

1.7.1 The population and its samples
The finite population, or universe, of \(N\) units is denoted by the index set \[
\mathcal{U} = \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}.
\] Out of this population we can choose various samples, which are subsets of \(\mathcal{U}\). The sample actually chosen is denoted \(\mathcal{S}\); it consists of \(n\) of the units in \(\mathcal U\).
For example, suppose \(\mathcal{U} = \{1,2,3,4\}\), so \(N=4\). There are \(\binom42 = 6\) different samples of size \(n=2\): \[
\mathcal{S}_1=\{1,2\},\quad \mathcal{S}_2=\{1,3\},\quad \mathcal{S}_3=\{1,4\},\quad
\mathcal{S}_4=\{2,3\},\quad \mathcal{S}_5=\{2,4\},\quad \mathcal{S}_6=\{3,4\}.
\]


1.7.2 Probability sampling
In probability sampling, each possible sample \(\mathcal{S}\) has a known probability \(P(\mathcal{S})\) of being chosen, and the probabilities of all possible samples sum to 1. The collection of these probabilities is the sampling design. One possible design for a sample of size 2 from \(\mathcal{U}=\{1,2,3,4\}\) is \[
P(\mathcal{S}_1)=\tfrac13,\quad P(\mathcal{S}_4)=\tfrac16,\quad P(\mathcal{S}_6)=\tfrac12,
\quad P(\mathcal{S}_2)=P(\mathcal{S}_3)=P(\mathcal{S}_5)=0 .
\] The probabilities are known before the sample is drawn. One way to carry out this design is to put six balls in a box, two labeled 1, one labeled 4 and three labeled 6, draw one ball at random, and take the sample \(\mathcal S_i\) whose label is drawn. An SRS is the special design in which all six samples have probability \(1/6\).


1.7.3 The values \(y_i\)
Let \(y_i\) be a characteristic of the \(i\)th unit in the population, such as the corn yield of farm \(i\):

We treat each \(y_i\) as a fixed quantity. If farm 723 is in the sample, its corn yield \(y_{723}\) is known exactly; if it is not, \(y_{723}\) is unknown but still fixed. The only randomness is in which units are selected. This is the design-based (or randomization) approach, followed by Lohr and by this book. (Scheaffer et al. use \(Y_i\) for a random variable and \(y_i\) for its value.)


1.7.4 Inclusion probabilities and sampling weights
Once a sampling design is chosen, each unit in the population has a known probability of appearing in the sample, its inclusion probability \[
\pi_i = P(\text{unit } i \text{ is in the sample}) = \sum_{\mathcal S \ni i} P(\mathcal S),
\tag{1.1}\] the sum of the probabilities of all possible samples that contain unit \(i\). In probability sampling all the \(\pi_i\) are known before the survey starts, and we assume \(\pi_i > 0\) for every unit, so that every unit has a chance to be observed.
For the design above, unit 1 belongs only to \(\mathcal S_1 = \{1,2\}\) among the samples with positive probability, so \[
\pi_1 = P(\{1,2\}) = \tfrac13, \qquad
\pi_2 = P(\{1,2\})+P(\{2,3\}) = \tfrac13+\tfrac16=\tfrac12,
\] \[
\pi_3 = P(\{2,3\})+P(\{3,4\}) = \tfrac16+\tfrac12=\tfrac23, \qquad
\pi_4 = P(\{3,4\}) = \tfrac12 .
\] The inclusion probabilities do not sum to 1. They sum to 2, because every sample contains \(n = 2\) units; in general \(\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i = n\) for a design with fixed sample size \(n\).
The sampling weight of unit \(i\) is \(w_i = 1/\pi_i\). It can be thought of as the number of population units that a sampled unit represents. For many sampling designs, the estimator of the population total can be written as \[
\hat t = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} w_i \, y_i = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \frac{y_i}{\pi_i}.
\] For an SRS, \(\pi_i = n/N\) and \(w_i = N/n\) for every unit; for the other designs in this book, the weights differ between units.


1.7.5 Population quantities
The quantities we want to estimate are characteristics of the fixed values \(y_1, \ldots, y_N\): \[
\textbf{total: } t = \sum_{i=1}^N y_i, \qquad
\textbf{mean: } \bar y_{U} = \frac{t}{N},
\] \[
\textbf{variance: } S^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\bar y_{U})^2, \qquad
\textbf{standard deviation: } S = \sqrt{S^2}.
\] Scheaffer et al. instead use \(\sigma^2 = \frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \bar y_{U})^2\), dividing by \(N\) rather than \(N-1\). The two differ only by the factor \((N-1)/N\).
Example: a population proportion. Let \(y_i = 1\) if unit \(i\) has some attribute and \(y_i = 0\) otherwise:

\] \[
S^2 = \frac{1}{5-1}\Big((1-0.4)^2\times 2 + (0-0.4)^2\times 3\Big) = 0.3 .
\] For a 0/1 variable, \(S^2 = \frac{N}{N-1}\,p(1-p)\) with \(p = \bar y_U\); here \(\frac54(0.4)(0.6) = 0.3\). As \(N\) grows, \(S^2 \to p(1-p)\).

1.7.6 Statistics and sampling distributions
A statistic is a function of the observations in the sample, used to estimate a population quantity. Since the sample is random, so is the statistic. Its sampling distribution is its distribution under repeated sampling: the values it takes over all possible samples, with the probabilities \(P(\mathcal S)\) of those samples.
For example, to estimate the total \(t\) we may use the sample mean scaled up by the population size, \[
\bar y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}} y_i, \qquad \hat t = N\bar y .
\] Take the devices population (\(\bar y_U = 4\), \(t = 16\)) with the sampling design of the previous sections. For each of the six possible samples of size 2 we can compute \(\bar y\):

1.7.7 Bias, variance and mean squared error
The sampling distribution tells us how good an estimator \(\hat\theta\) of a population quantity \(\theta\) is. Three summaries are used: \[
\text{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E(\hat\theta) - \theta, \qquad
V(\hat\theta) = E\big[(\hat\theta - E(\hat\theta))^2\big], \qquad
\text{MSE}(\hat\theta) = E\big[(\hat\theta - \theta)^2\big].
\] The variance measures the spread of the estimates around their own mean; the MSE measures their spread around the true value.
For \(\bar y\) in the example, \[
E(\bar y) = 3\times\tfrac13 + 4\times\tfrac16 + 5\times\tfrac12 = \frac{25}{6},
\qquad
\text{Bias}(\bar y) = \frac{25}{6} - 4 = \frac16 ,
\] \[
V(\bar y) = \Big(3-\tfrac{25}{6}\Big)^2\tfrac13 + \Big(4-\tfrac{25}{6}\Big)^2\tfrac16
   + \Big(5-\tfrac{25}{6}\Big)^2\tfrac12 = \frac{29}{36} \approx 0.8056,
\] \[
\text{MSE}(\bar y) = (3-4)^2\cdot\tfrac13 + (4-4)^2\cdot\tfrac16 + (5-4)^2\cdot\tfrac12 = \frac56 \approx 0.8333 .
\] The estimator is biased under this design. The design favours the sample \(\{3,4\}\), which contains the household with 6 devices, so \(\bar y\) tends to be too large. Correspondingly \(\hat t = 4\bar y\) has \(E(\hat t) = 50/3 \approx 16.67\), a bias of \(2/3\) for \(t = 16\).
MSE = Bias² + Variance. Adding and subtracting \(E(\hat\theta)\), \[
\text{MSE}(\hat\theta)
= E\Big[\big(\hat\theta - E(\hat\theta)\big) + \big(E(\hat\theta) - \theta\big)\Big]^2
= V(\hat\theta) + \big(\text{Bias}(\hat\theta)\big)^2 ,
\] because the cross term \(2\,\text{Bias}(\hat\theta)\,E\big[\hat\theta - E(\hat\theta)\big]\) is zero. In the example, \((1/6)^2 + 29/36 = 1/36 + 29/36 = 30/36 = 5/6\), which agrees with the direct calculation. In particular, when \(\hat\theta\) is unbiased, \(\text{MSE}(\hat\theta) = V(\hat\theta)\).
The same population under SRS. If instead all six samples have probability \(1/6\) (an SRS), the six values of \(\bar y\) are \(3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5\), so \(E(\bar y) = 4 = \bar y_U\): the estimator is now unbiased. Its variance is \(\frac16(1+1+0+0+1+1) = \frac23\), which agrees with the SRS formula \(\big(1-\frac nN\big)\frac{S^2}{n} = \frac12\cdot\frac{8/3}{2} = \frac23\) of Section 3.2. The short R enumeration below checks both designs.


Code
y <- c(2, 4, 4, 6)
samples <- combn(4, 2)                        # the 6 possible samples, one per column
ybar <- apply(samples, 2, function(s) mean(y[s]))
designs <- rbind(unequal = c(1/3, 0, 0, 1/6, 0, 1/2),
                 SRS     = rep(1/6, 6))
round(t(apply(designs, 1, function(P) {
  E <- sum(P * ybar)
  c(E = E, Bias = E - mean(y), V = sum(P * (ybar - E)^2), MSE = sum(P * (ybar - mean(y))^2))
})), 4)

SRS     4.0000 0.0000 0.6667 0.6667




1.7.8 Unbiased, precise and accurate
An estimator \(\hat t\) of \(t\) is

unbiased if \(E(\hat t) = t\);
precise if \(V(\hat t) = E\big[(\hat t - E[\hat t])^2\big]\) is small;
accurate if \(\text{MSE}(\hat t) = E\big[(\hat t - t)^2\big]\) is small.

Precision measures how close the estimates from different samples are to each other; accuracy measures how close they are to the truth. A badly biased estimator may be very precise but will not be accurate. Figure 1.8 shows the three cases as archers aiming at the centre of a target: archer A is unbiased but imprecise, archer B is precise but biased, and archer C is both unbiased and precise, and therefore accurate. Selection bias and measurement bias make a survey like archer B: increasing the sample size makes the estimates more precise, but no closer to the truth.






Figure 1.8: Unbiased but imprecise (A), precise but biased (B), and accurate (C).





1.7.9 Summary
The finite population \(\mathcal U\) consists of the units \(\{1,2,\ldots,N\}\), with values \(\{y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_N\}\). We select a sample \(\mathcal S\) of \(n\) units from \(\mathcal U\) using the selection probabilities that define the sampling design. The \(y_i\) are fixed but unknown quantities, unknown unless unit \(i\) happens to appear in the sample. All statements about the bias, variance and MSE of an estimator refer to its distribution over the possible samples. The following chapters work out these properties for each design, starting with simple random sampling in Section 3.1.

2.7 Writing your own function


Code
## data is a matrix or data frame; returns the mean of each column
means_col <- function(data) {
  n <- ncol(data)
  cmeans <- rep(NA_real_, n)
  for (j in seq_len(n)) {
    cmeans[j] <- mean(data[[j]], na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  names(cmeans) <- colnames(data)
  cmeans
}


Indexing with data[[j]] extracts column j as a vector for both data frames and tibbles, whereas data[, j] returns a one-column tibble in the tibble case. seq_len(n) is used in place of 1:n so that a zero-column input yields an empty loop rather than iterating over 1, 0.

title: 3  Simple Random Sampling
text:
3.1 SRS and SRSWR
Simple random sampling is the simplest probability sampling design, and the building block for all the designs in later chapters. A stratified sample is an SRS within each stratum; a cluster sample is an SRS of clusters. This chapter defines the design, derives its estimators and their standard errors, shows how to build confidence intervals and choose the sample size, and checks the theory by simulation. The material corresponds to Sections 2.3–2.6 and 2.8 of Lohr and Sections 4.1–4.5 of Scheaffer et al.
There are two versions of simple random sampling.
A simple random sample with replacement (SRSWR) of size \(n\) from a population of \(N\) units can be thought of as \(n\) independent draws of one unit, each unit having probability \(1/N\) on every draw. The same unit can be drawn more than once.
A simple random sample without replacement (SRS) of size \(n\) is selected so that every possible subset of \(n\) distinct units in the population has the same probability of being the sample. There are \(\binom{N}{n}\) such subsets, so \[
P(\mathcal S) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{n!\,(N-n)!}{N!}
\] for every subset \(\mathcal S\) of size \(n\). Unless stated otherwise, “SRS” in this book means sampling without replacement. In practice an SRS is drawn with computer-generated random numbers; in R,
Code
sample(1:N, size = n)
returns the labels of \(n\) distinct units chosen in this way.
Figure 3.1 illustrates an SRS of \(n = 60\) from a synthetic population of \(N = 1000\) units. The design uses no information about the units other than their labels, so the sampled units (red) are scattered at random over the population, and their values cover its whole range.
Figure 3.1: A simple random sample of \(n = 60\) (red) from a synthetic population of \(N = 1000\) units, listed in an arbitrary order. The dashed line is the population mean.

title: 3  Simple Random Sampling
text:
3.1.1 Inclusion probabilities
To study which units end up in the sample, define the sample-membership indicator \[
Z_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if unit } i \text{ is in the sample,} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\] The probability \(\pi_i = P(Z_i = 1)\) is the inclusion probability of unit \(i\). If unit \(i\) is in the sample, the other \(n-1\) sampled units must come from the remaining \(N-1\) units, so \[
\pi_i = P(Z_i=1) = \frac{\text{number of samples including unit } i}{\text{number of possible samples}}
= \frac{\binom{N-1}{n-1}}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{n}{N}.
\] Every unit has the same chance \(n/N\) of being in the sample. The indicators \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_N\) are the only random quantities in design-based inference; we use them in Section 3.6 to prove the properties of the estimators.

title: 3  Simple Random Sampling
text:
3.2 Estimators for Simple Random Sampling
Write \(y_i\) for the value of unit \(i\) in the population \(U = \{1, \ldots, N\}\), and \[
\bar{y}_U = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i, \qquad
t = \sum_{i=1}^N y_i = N\bar{y}_U, \qquad
S^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \bar{y}_U)^2
\] for the population mean, total and variance. These are fixed, unknown numbers.

3.2.1 Estimating the population mean
The natural estimator of \(\bar y_U\) is the sample mean, and the natural estimator of \(S^2\) is the sample variance: \[
\bar y = \frac1n \sum_{i \in \mathcal S} y_i = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^N Z_i y_i,
\qquad
s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} (y_i - \bar y)^2 .
\] The sample mean is unbiased for \(\bar y_U\), and its variance is \[
V(\bar{y}) = \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{S^2}{n}
\] (both are proved in Section 3.6). This is the familiar \(S^2/n\) of independent sampling, multiplied by the factor \(1 - n/N\), the finite population correction (fpc). Sampling without replacement removes units from the pool, so the sample covers more of the population than independent draws would, and the variance is smaller. When the sampling fraction \(n/N\) is small, the fpc is close to \(1\) and can be ignored. When \(n = N\), the sample is a census and \(V(\bar y) = 0\).
Since \(s^2\) is unbiased for \(S^2\) (also proved in Section 3.6), replacing \(S^2\) by \(s^2\) gives an unbiased estimator of the variance. Its square root is the standard error: \[
\boxed{
\hat{V}(\bar{y}) = \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{s^2}{n}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\bar y) = \sqrt{\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{s^2}{n}} .}
\]


3.2.2 Estimating the population total
Since \(t = N\bar y_U\), the total is estimated by scaling up the sample mean: \[
\boxed{
\hat{t} = N\bar{y}, \qquad
\hat{V}(\hat{t}) = N^2\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{s^2}{n}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat{t}) = N\,\mathrm{SE}(\bar{y}).}
\]
Sampling weights. The estimated total can also be written with sampling weights. The sampling weight of a unit is the reciprocal of its inclusion probability, \(w_i = 1/\pi_i = N/n\), and \[
\hat t = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S} w_i y_i = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \frac{N}{n} y_i .
\] Each sampled unit “represents” \(N/n\) units of the population: itself and \(N/n - 1\) unsampled ones. In an SRS all weights are equal; in later chapters (stratified, cluster and unequal-probability sampling) they are not, but the weighted-sum form of \(\hat t\) carries over.


3.2.3 Coefficient of variation
The standard error is in the units of \(y\). A scale-free measure of precision is the coefficient of variation (CV), defined when \(\bar y_U \ne 0\): \[
\mathrm{CV}(\bar y) = \frac{\sqrt{V(\bar y)}}{E(\bar y)}
= \sqrt{1-\frac nN}\ \frac{S}{\sqrt n\, \bar y_{U}},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{CV}}(\bar y) = \frac{\mathrm{SE}(\bar y)}{\bar y} .
\] Because \(\hat t = N\bar y\), the factor \(N\) cancels and \(\mathrm{CV}(\hat t) = \mathrm{CV}(\bar y)\). A CV of 0.05 means the standard error is 5% of the estimate, whatever the units of measurement.


3.2.4 Estimating a proportion
Estimating a proportion is a special case of estimating a mean. Define \(y_i=1\) if unit \(i\) has the characteristic of interest and \(y_i=0\) otherwise. Then the population proportion and the sample proportion are \[
p = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i = \bar y_{U}, \qquad
\hat p = \frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} y_i = \bar y ,
\] so \(\hat p\) is unbiased for \(p\). For a 0/1 variable \(y_i^2 = y_i\), and the variances simplify: \[
S^2 = \frac{N}{N-1}\,p(1-p), \qquad
s^2 = \frac{n}{n-1}\,\hat p(1-\hat p).
\] Substituting into the general formulas, \[
V(\hat p) = \Big(\frac{N-n}{N-1}\Big)\frac{p(1-p)}{n},
\qquad
\boxed{\hat V(\hat p) = \Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{\hat p (1-\hat p)}{n-1}.}
\] The number of units with the characteristic, \(Np\), is estimated by \(N\hat p\) with standard error \(N\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat p)\).

title: 3  Simple Random Sampling
text:
3.3 Example: The Census of Agriculture
The U.S. government conducts a Census of Agriculture every five years. It collects data on all farms (any place producing $1000 or more of agricultural products) in the 50 states, for each of the \(N=3078\) counties and county-equivalents. The file agpop.csv contains the 1982, 1987 and 1992 farm data for the whole population. An SRS of \(n=300\) counties was selected with computer-generated random numbers and saved as agsrs.csv. We use it to estimate the mean and total of acres92, the number of acres devoted to farms in 1992, and the proportion of counties with fewer than 200,000 acres in farms.
Throughout the agriculture examples in this book, county acreages are expressed in thousands of acres. The raw figures run into the millions, and every mean, variance and total reads far more easily on that scale. The helper acres_in_thousands() performs the conversion as the data are read.

3.3.1 Step-by-step calculation
We first compute the estimates directly from the formulas of Section 3.2.


Code
## read survey data

## work in thousands of acres, the unit used for every agriculture example here

head(agsrs)



  



Code

N <- 3078

## do calculation

ybar <- mean (sdata)
s <- sd (sdata)
se.ybar <- sqrt((1 - n / N)) * s / sqrt(n)
mem <- qt (0.975, df = n - 1) * se.ybar

## return estimate vector for pop mean
c (Est. = ybar, S.E. = se.ybar, ci.low = ybar - mem, ci.upp = ybar + mem)

In thousands of acres, the sample gives \(\bar y = 297.897\) and \(s = 344.55\), so \[
\mathrm{SE}(\bar y) = \sqrt{\Big(1-\frac{300}{3078}\Big)\frac{344.55^2}{300}} = 18.898,
\] \[
\hat t = N\bar y = 3078(297.897) = 916,927,
\qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat t) = 3078(18.898) = 58,169 .
\] The average county has about 298 thousand acres in farms, and the U.S. total is estimated at about 917 million acres. The estimated coefficient of variation is \[
\widehat{\mathrm{CV}}(\hat t) = \widehat{\mathrm{CV}}(\bar y)
= \frac{\mathrm{SE}(\bar y)}{\bar y}
= \frac{18.898}{297.897} = 0.0634,
\] so the standard error is about 6.3% of the estimate.
The data are highly skewed (Figure 3.2): most counties have fewer than 500 thousand acres in farms, but some have more than 1.5 million. For such data the mean is pulled up by the long right tail, and we should also report the median, which is 196.7 thousand acres here, well below the mean.

A proportion. Let \(y_i = 1\) if county \(i\) has fewer than 200 thousand acres in farms. In the sample, 153 of the 300 counties do, so \(\hat p = 153/300 = 0.51\) and \[

title: 3  Simple Random Sampling
text:
3.4 Confidence Intervals
A confidence interval (CI) indicates the accuracy of an estimate. A 95% CI is often explained heuristically: if we took samples from the population over and over again, and constructed a CI by our procedure for each possible sample, we would expect 95% of the resulting intervals to include the true value of the population quantity. In design-based inference this is literally what the probability refers to: the population is fixed and the randomness is over the \(\binom{N}{n}\) possible samples.

3.4.1 Normality of the sample mean
In an SRS without replacement the observations are not independent, so the ordinary central limit theorem does not apply directly. A finite-population version is due to Hájek (1960): if certain technical conditions hold and \(n\), \(N\) and \(N-n\) are all “sufficiently large”, then the sampling distribution of \[
\frac{\bar y - \bar y_{U}}{\sqrt{\big(1-\tfrac nN\big)}\, \tfrac{S}{\sqrt n}}
\] is approximately standard normal. Replacing \(S\) by \(s\) gives the standard error, and approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CIs for the mean, total and proportion are \[
\bar y \pm t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1} \, \mathrm{SE}(\bar y), \qquad
\hat t \pm t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1} \, \mathrm{SE}(\hat t), \qquad
\hat p \pm t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1} \, \mathrm{SE}(\hat p).
\] The \(t\) quantile is customary; for the sample sizes used in surveys it is very close to the normal quantile \(z_{\alpha/2}\).
Example (continued). For the agriculture sample, \(t_{0.025,\,299} = 1.968\), and the 95% CIs are \[
\text{mean: } 297.9 \pm 1.968(18.9) = [260.7,\ 335.1] \text{ thousand acres},
\] \[
\text{total: } [802,454,\ 1,031,400] \text{ thousand acres},
\] \[
\text{proportion: } 0.51 \pm 1.968(0.0275) = [0.456,\ 0.564],
\] matching the output of srs_est() in Section 3.3.


3.4.2 How large must \(n\) be for normality?
The normal approximation needs a larger sample when the population is skewed, as acreage is. Sugden, Smith and Jones (2000) extend Cochran’s rule and recommend the minimum sample size \[
n_{\min} = 28 + 25\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\bar y_{U})^3}{N S^3}\right)^{\!2},
\] where the quantity in parentheses is the skewness of the population. The more skewed the population, the larger the sample required.


Code
g1 <- (sum((sdata - ybar)^3) / n) / s^3   # sample skewness
n_min <- 28 + 25 * g1^2
c(skewness = g1, n_min = n_min)


  skewness      n_min 
  2.567866 192.848373 


For the agriculture data we substitute the sample quantities: \(s = 344.55\) and \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(y_i-\bar y)^3/n = 1.0504 \times 10^{8}\) (in thousands of acres), giving a skewness of 2.57 and \[
n_{\min} = 28 + 25(2.568)^2 \approx 193 .
\] Our sample of \(n=300\) exceeds \(n_{\min}\), so it appears large enough for the sampling distribution of \(\bar y\) to be approximately normal. The simulation in Section 3.7 confirms this.

title: 3  Simple Random Sampling
text:
3.5 Choosing the Sample Size
Before a survey is carried out we must decide how large the sample should be. The answer depends on how precise the estimate must be.

3.5.1 Specifying the tolerable error
The desired precision is often expressed in absolute terms, \[
P(|\bar y - \bar y_{U}| \le e) = 1-\alpha ,
\] where \(e\) is the margin of error. For many surveys of people that measure a proportion, \(e=0.03\) and \(\alpha=0.05\). Alternatively, precision can be specified in relative terms, which controls the CV: \[
P\left(\left|\frac{\bar y - \bar y_{U}}{\bar y_{U}}\right| \le r\right) = 1-\alpha,
\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad e = r \, \bar y_{U} .
\] For example, if \(\bar y_{U} \approx 180\) thousand and \(r=0.1\), then \(e=18\) thousand.


3.5.2 Solving for \(n\)
Using the normal approximation, the margin of error is \(z_{\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{SD}(\bar y)\), so we need \(n\) with \[
e = z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{S^2}{n}} .
\] Solving in two steps is convenient. First find the sample size \(n_0\) we would need for an infinite population (no fpc): \[
n_0 = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\, S}{e}\right)^{\!2}.
\] Then adjust for the finite population: \[
\boxed{n = \frac{n_0}{1+n_0/N} = \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 S^2}{e^2 + z_{\alpha/2}^2 S^2/N}.}
\] When \(N\) is large relative to \(n_0\), \(n \approx n_0\); the population size matters only when \(n_0\) is a substantial fraction of \(N\). The formula needs a value for \(S\), which is unknown. It can come from a pilot sample, a previous survey of a similar population, or a guess. For a proportion, \(S^2 \approx p(1-p) \le 1/4\), so using \(p = 1/2\) gives a conservative (largest) sample size.


Code
srs_size <- function(S, e, N = Inf, alpha = 0.05) {
  n0 <- (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) * S / e)^2
  c(n0 = n0, n = n0 / (1 + n0 / N))
}


Example: margin of error 0.03 for a proportion. We want to estimate the proportion of the \(N=1251\) recipes in a cookbook that do not involve animal products, with a 95% CI of margin of error 0.03. Using the conservative \(p = 1/2\), \[
n_0 = \frac{(1.96)^2 (\tfrac12)(1-\tfrac12)}{(0.03)^2} \approx 1067 .
\] Since \(n_0\) is large relative to \(N=1251\), the fpc adjustment matters: \[
n = \frac{n_0}{1+n_0/N} = \frac{1067}{1+1067/1251} \approx 576 .
\] If \(N\) were very large we would use \(n\approx n_0 = 1067\).


Code
srs_size(S = 0.5, e = 0.03, N = 1251)


       n0         n 
1067.0719  575.8695 


Example: the agriculture survey. A pilot sample of 30 counties was taken (one county was missing acres92). The sample SD of the remaining 29 observations was 519.085 thousand acres. With a desired margin of error of 60 thousand acres, \[
n_0 = (1.96)^2\,\frac{519.085^2}{60^2} \approx 288,
\qquad
n = \frac{288}{1+288/3078} \approx 263 .
\] The investigators took a sample of 300, in case the pilot’s estimate of the SD was too low.


Code
srs_size(S = 519.085, e = 60, N = 3078)


      n0        n 
287.5217 262.9583

title: 3  Simple Random Sampling
text:
3.6 Randomization Theory for SRS
We now prove the properties of \(\bar y\) and \(s^2\) used above. In the randomization theory (design-based) approach, the values \(y_1, \ldots, y_N\) are fixed but unknown numbers. The only random variables are the indicators \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_N\) that record which units are in the sample: \[
\bar y = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \frac{y_i}{n} = \sum_{i=1}^N Z_i \frac{y_i}{n} .
\] All the randomness in \(\bar y\) comes from \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\).

3.6.1 Moments of \(Z_i\)
Each \(Z_i\) is a Bernoulli random variable with \(P(Z_i=1) = \pi_i = n/N\) (Section 3.1). Since \(Z_i^2 = Z_i\), \[
E[Z_i] = E[Z_i^2] = \frac nN, \qquad
V(Z_i) = \frac nN - \Big(\frac nN\Big)^2 = \frac nN\Big(1-\frac nN\Big).
\] The \(Z_i\) are not independent, because the sample size is fixed: if unit \(i\) is in the sample, there is one less place for the other units. For \(i\ne j\), given that unit \(i\) is sampled, the remaining \(n-1\) units are an SRS from the other \(N-1\), so \[
E[Z_iZ_j] = P(Z_j=1\mid Z_i=1)\,P(Z_i=1) = \frac{n-1}{N-1}\cdot\frac nN ,
\] \[
\mathrm{Cov}(Z_i,Z_j) = E[Z_iZ_j]-E[Z_i]E[Z_j]
= \frac nN\Big(\frac{n-1}{N-1} - \frac nN\Big)
= -\frac{1}{N-1}\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac nN .
\] This negative covariance is the source of the finite population correction.


3.6.2 Unbiasedness of \(\bar y\)
By linearity of expectation, \[
E[\bar y] = \sum_{i=1}^N E[Z_i]\frac{y_i}{n}
= \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{n}{N}\cdot\frac{y_i}{n}
= \frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N y_i = \bar y_{U}.
\] So \(\bar y\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\bar y_{U}\), and \(\hat t = N\bar y\) is unbiased for \(t\).


3.6.3 Variance of \(\bar y\)
Expanding the variance of a sum, \[
\begin{aligned}
V(\bar y) &= \frac{1}{n^2}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2\, V(Z_i) + \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j\ne i} y_i y_j\,\mathrm{Cov}(Z_i,Z_j)\right] \\
&= \frac{1}{n^2}\,\frac nN\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\left[\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2 - \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j\ne i} y_i y_j\right].
\end{aligned}
\] Using \(\sum_i\sum_{j\ne i} y_iy_j = \big(\sum_i y_i\big)^2 - \sum_i y_i^2\), the term in brackets is \[
\frac{N\sum_{i} y_i^2 - \big(\sum_{i} y_i\big)^2}{N-1}
= \frac{N\sum_i (y_i - \bar y_U)^2}{N-1} = N S^2 .
\] Therefore \[
V(\bar y) = \frac{1}{n^2}\,\frac nN\Big(1-\frac nN\Big) N S^2 = \Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{S^2}{n}.
\] Without the negative covariances, the result would be \(\frac{N-1}{N}\cdot\frac{S^2}{n}\) (the SRSWR variance). The covariance terms produce the factor \(1 - n/N\).


3.6.4 Unbiasedness of \(s^2\)
Adding and subtracting \(\bar y_U\) inside the sum of squares gives the identity \[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(y_i-\bar y)^2 = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(y_i-\bar y_{U})^2 - n(\bar y - \bar y_U)^2 .
\] Take expectations. For the first term, \(E\big[\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i(y_i-\bar y_U)^2\big] = \frac nN (N-1)S^2\); for the second, \(E[n(\bar y - \bar y_U)^2] = nV(\bar y) = (1-\frac nN)S^2\). Hence \[
E\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(y_i-\bar y)^2\right]
= \frac{n(N-1)}{N}S^2 - \frac{N-n}{N}S^2 = (n-1)S^2 ,
\] and therefore \(E[s^2] = S^2\). It follows that \(\hat V(\bar y) = (1-\frac nN)\frac{s^2}{n}\) is unbiased for \(V(\bar y)\). (The standard error, its square root, is slightly biased, as a square root always is, but this is ignored in practice.)

title: 3  Simple Random Sampling
section: 3.7 A Simulation Demonstration of SRS Inference
text:
3.7 A Simulation Demonstration of SRS Inference
The theory says that \(\bar y\) is unbiased, that its standard deviation is \(\sqrt{1-n/N}\,S/\sqrt n\), that it is approximately normal for \(n = 300\), and that the 95% CIs cover \(\bar y_U\) about 95% of the time. Because agpop.csv contains the whole population, we can check all four claims by drawing many samples from it.


Code
# read population data, with acreages in thousands of acres
agpop <- acres_in_thousands (read.csv ("data/agpop.csv"))
# remove those counties with na
agpop <- subset( agpop, !is.na (acres92))



3.7.1 True values
We fix the sample size and compute the true population mean and the true standard deviation of \(\bar y\) from the population \(S\): \[
\mathrm{SD}(\bar{y}) = \sqrt{1 - \frac{n}{N}} \left(\frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]


Code
# sample size
n <- 300
# population size
N <- nrow (agpop); N

# true value of population mean
ybarU <- mean (agpop[,"acres92"]); ybarU


[1] 308.5824

A single random sample of \(n=300\), analyzed with srs_est(), is one instance of survey inference:

head(agpop [srs, ])

title: 4  Stratified Random Sampling
text:
4.1 What Is Stratified Sampling?
Suppose the variable we are interested in has different means in different subpopulations. Then a stratified random sample can often give more precise estimates of population quantities than a simple random sample of the same size. The word stratify comes from Latin words meaning “to make layers”. We divide the population of \(N\) units into \(H\) subpopulations, called strata. The strata do not overlap and together they make up the whole population, so each sampling unit belongs to exactly one stratum. We then draw an independent probability sample from each stratum and pool the information to estimate population quantities.
Figure 4.1 illustrates the design on a synthetic population of \(N = 1000\) units in \(H = 4\) strata of sizes \(N_h = 400, 300, 200\) and \(100\), sorted by their means. The sample of \(n = 60\) is allocated in proportion to the stratum sizes, \(n_h = 60 N_h/N = 24, 18, 12\) and \(6\), and an SRS of \(n_h\) units is drawn in each stratum, so every stratum is represented in the sample. Because the stratum means are far apart while the spread within each stratum is small, most of the variation in the population lies between the strata, and this part of the variation does not affect the stratified estimator (Section 4.2).
Figure 4.1: A stratified random sample from a synthetic population of \(N = 1000\) units in \(H = 4\) strata of sizes \(N_h = 400, 300, 200, 100\), sorted by their means (dashed lines). An SRS of \(n_h = 24, 18, 12, 6\) units (red) is drawn in each stratum (proportional allocation).
In this chapter the sample within each stratum is a simple random sample (SRS), drawn without replacement. The design is then called stratified random sampling. The material corresponds to Sections 3.1–3.5 of Lohr and Sections 5.1–5.9 of Scheaffer et al.
Example: stratifying U.S. counties by census region. In the SRS chapter we sampled about 10% of the 3078 U.S. counties to estimate the average farm acreage per county. Here we use the four U.S. census regions as strata. To compare stratified sampling directly with SRS, we again sample about 10% of the counties, this time 10% of the counties in each stratum:
We select four separate, independent SRSs, one per stratum. Knowing which counties are in the sample from the Northeast tells us nothing about which counties are in the sample from the South. We analyze these data in Section 4.6.1.

title: 4  Stratified Random Sampling
text:
4.2 Estimation with Stratified Samples

4.2.1 Population quantities
Let \(y_{hj}\) be the value of unit \(j\) in stratum \(h\), for \(j = 1, \ldots, N_h\) and \(h = 1, \ldots, H\), so that \(N = \sum_{h=1}^H N_h\). The stratum weight \[
\pi_h = \frac{N_h}{N}
\] is the proportion of population units in stratum \(h\), so \(\sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h = 1\). The population quantities of each stratum, and of the whole population, are \[
t_h = \sum_{j=1}^{N_h} y_{hj} \quad(\text{stratum total}), \qquad
t = \sum_{h=1}^H t_h \quad(\text{population total}),
\] \[
\overline y_{hU} = \frac{t_h}{N_h} \quad(\text{stratum mean}), \qquad
\overline y_U = \frac tN = \sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h\, \overline y_{hU} \quad(\text{overall mean}),
\] \[
S_h^2 = \frac{1}{N_h-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N_h}(y_{hj}-\overline y_{hU})^2 \quad(\text{stratum variance}).
\] The overall mean \(\overline y_U\) is the average of the stratum means, weighted by the stratum weights.


4.2.2 SRS estimators within each stratum
Let \(\mathcal S_h\) be the SRS of \(n_h\) units drawn from stratum \(h\), with total sample size \(n = \sum_{h=1}^H n_h\). Within stratum \(h\) we have an ordinary SRS, so we estimate the stratum quantities with the SRS formulas, applied separately to each stratum: \[
\overline y_h = \frac{1}{n_h}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} y_{hj}, \qquad
\hat t_h = \frac{N_h}{n_h}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} y_{hj} = N_h \overline y_h, \qquad
s_h^2 = \frac{1}{n_h - 1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} (y_{hj}-\overline y_h)^2 .
\]


4.2.3 Estimators for the population total and mean
Adding up the estimated stratum totals gives the stratified estimator of the population total. Dividing it by \(N\) gives the estimator of the population mean: \[
\boxed{
\hat t_{\text{str}} = \sum_{h=1}^H \hat t_h = \sum_{h=1}^H N_h \overline y_h,
\qquad
\overline y_{\text{str}} = \frac{\hat t_{\text{str}}}{N} = \sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h\overline y_h .}
\] So \(\overline y_{\text{str}}\) is a weighted average of the stratum sample means, with \(\overline y_h\) weighted by \(\pi_h = N_h/N\), the fraction of population units in stratum \(h\). To use stratified sampling, the stratum sizes \(N_h\) must be known.
Unbiasedness. Since an SRS is taken in each stratum, \(E[\overline y_h]=\overline y_{hU}\). Averaging these unbiased stratum estimates with the fixed weights \(N_h/N\) keeps the overall estimate unbiased: \[
E[\overline y_{\text{str}}]
= \sum_{h=1}^H \frac{N_h}{N}E[\overline y_h]
= \sum_{h=1}^H \frac{N_h}{N}\cdot \frac{1}{N_h}\sum_{j=1}^{N_h} y_{hj}
= \frac1N\sum_{h=1}^H \sum_{j=1}^{N_h}y_{hj} = \overline y_U .
\] It follows that \(E[\hat t_{\text{str}}] = N\,\overline y_U = t\).


4.2.4 Variances and standard errors
The strata are sampled independently, so the \(\hat t_h\) are independent and their variances add. Each \(\hat t_h\) has the SRS variance \(N_h^2(1-n_h/N_h)S_h^2/n_h\), so \[
V(\hat t_{\text{str}}) = \sum_{h=1}^H V(\hat t_h) = \sum_{h=1}^H \Big(1-\frac{n_h}{N_h}\Big)N_h^2\frac{S_h^2}{n_h},
\qquad
V(\overline y_{\text{str}}) = \frac{V(\hat t_{\text{str}})}{N^2} = \sum_{h=1}^H \Big(1-\frac{n_h}{N_h}\Big)\pi_h^2 \frac{S_h^2}{n_h}.
\] Only the variability within the strata enters these variances. The differences between the stratum means do not. This is the source of the gain from stratification: if the strata are internally homogeneous, every \(S_h^2\) is small, even when the population as a whole is very variable.
Substituting the sample variances \(s_h^2\) for \(S_h^2\) gives unbiased variance estimators, and their square roots are the standard errors: \[
\boxed{
\hat V(\overline y_{\text{str}}) = \sum_{h=1}^H v_h, \qquad
v_h = \Big(1-\frac{n_h}{N_h}\Big)\pi_h^2\frac{s_h^2}{n_h}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\overline y_{\text{str}}) = \sqrt{\hat V(\overline y_{\text{str}})} ,}
\] \[
\hat V(\hat t_{\text{str}}) = N^2\,\hat V(\overline y_{\text{str}}) = \sum_{h=1}^H \Big(1-\frac{n_h}{N_h}\Big)N_h^2\frac{s_h^2}{n_h},
\qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat t_{\text{str}}) = N\,\mathrm{SE}(\overline y_{\text{str}}).
\] Here \(v_h\) is the contribution of stratum \(h\) to the estimated variance. It appears as the last column of the working tables in this chapter. Each stratum needs at least two sampled units, \(n_h \ge 2\), so that \(s_h^2\) can be computed.


4.2.5 Confidence intervals
Suppose either the sample sizes within the strata are large, or the design has a large number of strata. Then \(\overline y_{\text{str}}\) is approximately normal, and an approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\overline y_U\) is \[
\overline y_{\text{str}} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\overline y_{\text{str}}).
\] When \(n\) is not large, it is common to replace the normal quantile by the quantile of a \(t\) distribution with \(n-H\) degrees of freedom, for example \(\hat t_{\text{str}} \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-H}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat t_{\text{str}})\) for the total. The functions used in this book use \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\).

4.4 Stratified Sampling for Proportions
A proportion is the mean of a 0/1 variable. So we can apply the same formulas with \(\overline y_h = \hat p_h\), the sample proportion in stratum \(h\), and \(s_h^2 = \frac{n_h}{n_h-1}\hat p_h(1-\hat p_h)\): \[
\boxed{\hat p_{\text{str}} = \sum_{h=1}^H \frac{N_h}{N}\hat p_h, \qquad
\hat V(\hat p_{\text{str}}) = \sum_{h=1}^H \Big(1-\frac{n_h}{N_h}\Big)\Big(\frac{N_h}{N}\Big)^2\frac{\hat p_h(1-\hat p_h)}{n_h-1}}.
\] The total number of units with the attribute is estimated by \(N\hat p_{\text{str}}\), with standard error \(N\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat p_{\text{str}})\).

title: 4  Stratified Random Sampling
text:
4.5 Alternative Formulas for \(\overline y_{\text{str}}\)
The estimator \(\overline y_{\text{str}} = \sum_h \pi_h \overline y_h\) can be written in two other ways. Each one shows something about the design. The first compares it with the sample mean of an SRS and shows why the weights must be \(N_h/N\). The second writes it as a weighted average over individual units, with each unit weighted by its sampling weight. This is the form used for survey data files.

4.5.1 Weighting by population fractions instead of sample fractions
Suppose instead that we had taken an SRS of size \(n=n_1+\cdots+n_H\) from the whole population. Grouping the sampled units by stratum, the sample mean is \[
\overline y_{\text{SRS}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{(h,j)\in\mathcal S} y_{hj}
= \frac{n_1\overline y_1 + \cdots + n_H\overline y_H}{n}
= \overline y_1\frac{n_1}{n} + \cdots + \overline y_H\frac{n_H}{n},
\] which we compare with the stratified estimator \[
\overline y_{\text{str}} = \overline y_1\frac{N_1}{N} + \cdots + \overline y_H\frac{N_H}{N}.
\] For proportions, similarly, \(\hat p_{\text{SRS}} = \sum_{h} \frac{n_h}{n}\hat p_h\) while \(\hat p_{\text{str}} = \sum_{h} \frac{N_h}{N}\hat p_h\).
Both estimators average the stratum sample means. The difference is in the weights. In an SRS, the stratum sizes in the sample \(n_h\) are random, so \(\overline y_{\text{SRS}}\) weights each stratum by its realized sample fraction \(n_h/n\). That fraction varies from sample to sample and can be distorted by nonresponse rates that differ between strata. In contrast, \(\overline y_{\text{str}}\) uses the known, fixed population fraction \(N_h/N\). These fixed weights make it unbiased for \(\overline y_U\) whatever the \(n_h\) are. When \(n_h/n = N_h/N\) for every \(h\) (proportional allocation, Section 4.7), the two estimators coincide.


4.5.2 Weighting each unit by its sampling weight
Write the stratified sample as \(\mathcal S = (\mathcal S_1,\ldots,\mathcal S_H)\), where \(\mathcal S_h\) is the SRS drawn from stratum \(h\). The strata are sampled independently, so the probability of selecting a particular sample is the product of the probabilities of its stratum samples: \[
P(\mathcal S) = P(\mathcal S_1)\times P(\mathcal S_2)\times\cdots\times P(\mathcal S_H)
= \frac{1}{\binom{N_1}{n_1}}\cdot\frac{1}{\binom{N_2}{n_2}}\cdots\frac{1}{\binom{N_H}{n_H}}.
\]
For SRS we defined the sampling weight of a unit as the reciprocal of its inclusion probability. A unit \(j\) in stratum \(h\) is included with probability \(n_h/N_h\), the sampling fraction in stratum \(h\). (Do not confuse this with the stratum weight \(\pi_h = N_h/N\).) So its sampling weight is \[
w_{hj} = \frac{N_h}{n_h}.
\] Unless every stratum has the same sampling fraction, units in different strata have different inclusion probabilities. Stratified sampling is therefore an example of unequal-probability sampling.
The sampling weight can be thought of as the number of population units that a sampled unit represents. Within stratum \(h\) all \(n_h\) sampled units have the same weight \(N_h/n_h\), so the weights add up to the stratum sizes and to the population size: \[
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} w_{hj} = n_h\cdot\frac{N_h}{n_h} = N_h,
\qquad
\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} w_{hj} = \sum_{h=1}^H N_h = N.
\]
Estimators in terms of the weights. Since \(N_h\overline y_h = \frac{N_h}{n_h}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} y_{hj} = \sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} w_{hj}\,y_{hj}\), the estimated total is a weighted sum over all sampled units, regardless of stratum. Since the weights sum to \(N\), the estimated mean is a weighted average: \[
\hat t_{\text{str}} = \sum_{h=1}^H \sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} w_{hj}\, y_{hj},
\qquad
\overline y_{\text{str}} = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} w_{hj}y_{hj}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_h} w_{hj}}.
\] This is how survey data files are usually distributed: one row per sampled unit, with a column of sampling weights. The weight column of agstrat.csv in Section 4.6.1 is an example.
For the caribou survey the weights are:



Stratum

Section 4.10 repeats the comparison over thousands of samples.

title: 4  Stratified Random Sampling
text:
4.7 Efficiency of Proportional Allocation
So far the stratum sample sizes \(n_h\) were given. How should a total sample of size \(n\) be divided among the strata? We first study a simple benchmark, proportional allocation, which uses the same sampling fraction in every stratum: \[
\frac{n_h}{N_h} = \frac nN \quad \text{for all } h, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad n_h = n\,\frac{N_h}{N} = n\pi_h .
\] Then every unit has the same inclusion probability \(n/N\) and the same sampling weight \(N/n\), so the sample is self-weighting, and \(\overline y_{\text{str}}\) equals the plain sample mean. The county sample in Section 4.1, with about 10% of each region, is an example. Proportional allocation is not optimal in general (Section 4.8), but it lets us see clearly when, and by how much, stratification beats SRS.

4.7.1 Decomposition of the population variance
The answer depends on how the population variance splits into a part between the strata and a part within them. This is the decomposition of one-way analysis of variance:








Source
df
Sum of squares




Between strata
\(H-1\)
\(\text{SSB} = \sum_{h=1}^H N_h(\overline y_{hU}-\overline y_U)^2\)


Within strata
\(N-H\)
\(\text{SSW} = \sum_{h=1}^H (N_h-1)S_h^2 = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{j=1}^{N_h}(y_{hj}-\overline y_{hU})^2\)


Total, about \(\overline y_U\)
\(N-1\)
\(\text{SSTO} = (N-1)S^2 = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{j=1}^{N_h}(y_{hj}-\overline y_U)^2\)



\[
\text{SSTO} = \text{SSB} + \text{SSW}.
\]
One way to see the decomposition is to view each sum of squares as the squared length of a vector of prediction errors. Stack all \(N\) values into a vector \(\boldsymbol y\), and consider two ways of predicting them: \[
\begin{array}{c|ccc|c|ccc}
& & \text{stratum } 1 & & \cdots & & \text{stratum } H & \\ \hline
\boldsymbol y^\top & y_{11} & \cdots & y_{1N_1} & \cdots & y_{H1} & \cdots & y_{HN_H}\\
\hat{\boldsymbol y}_0^\top & \overline y_U & \cdots & \overline y_U & \cdots & \overline y_U & \cdots & \overline y_U\\
\hat{\boldsymbol y}_1^\top & \overline y_{1U} & \cdots & \overline y_{1U} & \cdots & \overline y_{HU} & \cdots & \overline y_{HU}
\end{array}
\] The prediction \(\hat{\boldsymbol y}_0\) ignores the strata and predicts every unit by the overall mean. The prediction \(\hat{\boldsymbol y}_1\) predicts each unit by its stratum mean. Then \[
\text{SSTO} = \|\boldsymbol y-\hat{\boldsymbol y}_0\|^2,\qquad
\text{SSW} = \|\boldsymbol y-\hat{\boldsymbol y}_1\|^2,\qquad
\text{SSB} = \|\hat{\boldsymbol y}_1-\hat{\boldsymbol y}_0\|^2 .
\] Since \(\boldsymbol y-\hat{\boldsymbol y}_0 = (\boldsymbol y-\hat{\boldsymbol y}_1) + (\hat{\boldsymbol y}_1-\hat{\boldsymbol y}_0)\), and the two pieces are orthogonal, the Pythagorean theorem gives \(\text{SSTO} = \text{SSW} + \text{SSB}\). The pieces are orthogonal because, within each stratum, the deviations \(y_{hj}-\overline y_{hU}\) sum to zero while \(\overline y_{hU}-\overline y_U\) is constant. Figure 4.3 illustrates the two predictions.








Figure 4.3: Left: predicting every unit by the overall mean (green dashed line); the squared errors (grey) sum to SSTO. Right: predicting each unit by its stratum mean (red segments); the squared errors sum to SSW. The difference SSTO − SSW is SSB.







4.7.2 The coefficient of determination \(R^2\)
The share of the total variation that is between strata is the coefficient of determination \[
R^2 = \frac{\text{SSB}}{\text{SSTO}} = 1-\frac{\text{SSW}}{\text{SSTO}} .
\] \(R^2\) generalizes the squared Pearson correlation coefficient. It measures how strongly a response \(y\) is related to one or more predictors. Here the predictor is “stratum membership”, and \(R^2\) is the proportion of the variance in \(y\) explained by the strata. It is the \(R^2\) of a regression of \(y\) on the stratum indicators, as in the ANOVA fits of Section 4.10. When the stratum means differ widely relative to the spread within each stratum, \(R^2\) is large (Figure 4.4, left). When the stratum means are nearly equal, \(R^2\) is small (right).








Figure 4.4: Strata with widely separated means (left, \(R^2\) large) and with nearly equal means (right, \(R^2\) small). Red segments are the stratum means.







4.7.3 Comparing the variances of proportional allocation and SRS
Under proportional allocation, \(1 - n_h/N_h = 1-n/N\) and \(N_h^2/n_h = (N/n)N_h\) for every stratum. So the variance of \(\hat t_{\text{str}}\) becomes \[
V_{\text{prop}}(\hat t_{\text{str}}) = \Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac Nn \sum_{h=1}^H N_h S_h^2
= \Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac Nn\left(\text{SSW} + \sum_{h=1}^H S_h^2\right),
\] using \(\sum_h N_hS_h^2 = \sum_h (N_h-1)S_h^2 + \sum_h S_h^2\). Equivalently, for the mean, \[
\boxed{V_{\text{prop}}(\overline y_{\text{str}}) = \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{1}{n}\sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h S_h^2},
\] a weighted average of the within-stratum variances in place of the overall \(S^2\). For an SRS of the same size \(n\), since \((N-1)S^2 = \text{SSTO} = \text{SSW}+\text{SSB}\), \[
V_{\text{SRS}}(\hat t) = \Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{N^2 S^2}{n}
= \Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{N}{n}\cdot\frac{N}{N-1}\,(\text{SSW}+\text{SSB}).
\]
When does stratification help? Comparing the two expressions, \(V_{\text{prop}} < V_{\text{SRS}}\) exactly when \((N-1)\big(\text{SSW} + \sum_h S_h^2\big) < N(\text{SSW}+\text{SSB})\). Substituting \(\text{SSW} = \sum_h(N_h-1)S_h^2\) and simplifying, the condition becomes \[
\text{SSB} > \sum_{h=1}^H \Big(1-\frac{N_h}{N}\Big)S_h^2 .
\] This almost always holds. SSB is a sum of \(N\) squared deviations, one for each unit in the population. The right side has only \(H\) terms, typically far fewer. Proportional allocation can lose to SRS only when the stratum means are almost identical, and even then the loss is negligible. In practice stratification with proportional allocation is never worse than SRS, up to terms of order \(1/N_h\).
How much does it help? Dropping the small terms \(\sum_h S_h^2\) and \(N/(N-1)\), the ratio of the variances is \[
\frac{V_{\text{prop}}(\hat t_{\text{str}})}{V_{\text{SRS}}(\hat t)}
\approx \frac{\text{SSW}+\sum_h S_h^2}{\text{SSW}+\text{SSB}} \approx \frac{\text{SSW}}{\text{SSTO}} = 1 - R^2,
\] so that \[
\boxed{\text{percentage of variance reduction} \approx \frac{\text{SSB}}{\text{SSTO}} = R^2_{y\mid\text{strata}}},
\] the proportion of the variance of \(y\) explained by stratum membership. The better the strata separate the values of \(y\), the larger the gain. We verify this relation by simulation in Section 4.10.

title: 4  Stratified Random Sampling
text:
4.8 Optimal Allocation

4.8.1 The cost function
The aim of optimal allocation is to gain the most information for the least cost. Let \(C\) be the total cost of the survey, \(c_0\) the overhead cost, and \(c_h\) the cost of sampling one unit in stratum \(h\): \[
C = c_0 + \sum_{h=1}^H c_h n_h .
\] We want to choose \(n_1,\ldots,n_H\) to minimize \(V(\overline y_{\text{str}})\) for a fixed total cost \(C\), or, equivalently, to minimize \(C\) for a fixed variance.


4.8.2 Derivation
Expanding the fpc, the variance separates into a part that depends on the \(n_h\) and a part that does not: \[
V(\overline y_{\text{str}}) = \sum_{h=1}^H \Big(1-\frac{n_h}{N_h}\Big)\frac{N_h^2}{N^2}\frac{S_h^2}{n_h}
= \sum_{h=1}^H \frac{N_h^2S_h^2}{N^2}\cdot\frac1{n_h} \;-\; \underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^H \frac{N_hS_h^2}{N^2}}_{\text{free of } n_h}.
\] We minimize the first sum subject to \(c_0+\sum_h c_hn_h = C\), using the Lagrangian \[
L(n_1,\ldots,n_H,\lambda) = \sum_{h=1}^H \frac{N_h^2S_h^2}{N^2 n_h} + \lambda\Big(c_0+\sum_{h=1}^H c_hn_h - C\Big).
\] Setting \(\partial L/\partial n_h = 0\) gives \[
-\frac{N_h^2S_h^2}{N^2n_h^2} + \lambda c_h = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
n_h = \frac{1}{N\sqrt\lambda}\cdot\frac{N_hS_h}{\sqrt{c_h}} .
\] Summing over \(h\) gives \(n = \frac{1}{N\sqrt\lambda}\sum_{l} N_lS_l/\sqrt{c_l}\). Dividing \(n_h\) by \(n\) eliminates \(\lambda\).


4.8.3 The optimal allocation
The optimal \(n_h\) is proportional to \(N_hS_h/\sqrt{c_h}\): \[
\boxed{
n_h = \left(\frac{N_hS_h/\sqrt{c_h}}{\sum_{l=1}^H N_lS_l/\sqrt{c_l}}\right)n,
\qquad n_h \propto \frac{N_hS_h}{\sqrt{c_h}} .}
\] The total \(n\) itself follows from the budget, or from a target variance. The formula says to sample more heavily in a stratum when:

the stratum is a large part of the population (\(N_h\) large);
the stratum is more variable (\(S_h\) large); or
sampling in the stratum is cheap (\(c_h\) small).

Two special cases are important. If the costs are equal, \(c_1=\cdots=c_H\), then \(n_h\propto N_hS_h\). This is Neyman allocation: \[
\boxed{n_h = n \frac{N_h S_h}{\sum_{l=1}^H N_l S_l}},
\] which gives the smallest possible variance for a total sample size \(n\): \[
\boxed{V_{\text{opt}}(\overline{y}_{\text{str}}) = \frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h S_h\right)^2 - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h S_h^2}.
\] If, in addition, the stratum standard deviations are equal, \(S_1=\cdots=S_H\), then \(n_h\propto N_h\), which is proportional allocation. Neyman allocation improves on proportional allocation exactly when the \(S_h\) differ across strata.
In practice the \(S_h\) are unknown when the survey is designed. They are replaced by estimates from a previous survey or a pilot sample, or by rough guesses. The allocation is fairly robust to such guesses: moderately wrong values of \(S_h\) still give a variance close to the optimum.

4.8.6 Example: Optimal allocation for polls
For estimating a proportion, \(S_h^2 \approx p_h(1-p_h)\). As a function of \(p\), \(p(1-p)\) is a quadratic maximized at \(p=1/2\) (Figure 4.5). Election regions where support is near 50%, the “swing states”, contribute the most variance per unit sampled. Optimal allocation therefore gives them relatively larger samples. The curve is flat near its maximum: \(p(1-p)\) is 0.21 at \(p = 0.3\) and still 0.25 at \(p = 0.5\). So Neyman allocation for proportions differs much from proportional allocation only when some \(p_h\) are close to 0 or 1.








Figure 4.5: The variance of a 0/1 variable, \(p(1-p)\), is largest at \(p = 0.5\).







4.8.7 Example: Dollar stratification
Dollar stratification is common in accounting audits. The recorded book amounts are used to stratify the population. For example, stratum 1 might be all loans over $1 million, stratum 2 the loans between $500,000 and $999,999, and so on, down to loans under $10,000. Optimal allocation is very efficient here. \(S_h\) is much larger in the strata with large loan amounts, so optimal allocation gives those strata a much higher sampling fraction. Often the top stratum is sampled completely (\(n_h = N_h\)). This makes sense: an error in a $3,000,000 loan is likely to contribute far more to the total audited discrepancy than an error in a $3,000 loan.

title: 4  Stratified Random Sampling
text:
4.9 Choosing Stratification Variables
Stratification is most efficient when the stratum means differ widely. Then SSB is large and the variability within the strata is small. Ideally we would stratify by the values of \(y\) itself. But \(y\) is unknown before sampling, so we look instead for an auxiliary variable \(x\) that is known for every unit in the population and is highly correlated with \(y\). Cutting the range of \(x\) into intervals then produces strata whose distributions of \(y\) differ (Figure 4.6).








Figure 4.6: Cutting an auxiliary variable \(x\) at its terciles (left, dashed lines) produces strata with visibly different distributions of \(y\) (right).





Some examples:

To estimate total business expenditure on advertising, we would like the businesses that spend the most on advertising in stratum 1, the next highest spenders in stratum 2, and so on. We might stratify by the number of employees or the size of the business, and by the type of product or service.
For farm income, we might use farm size as the stratification variable, since we expect larger farms to have higher incomes.
For the county farm data, the acreage in an earlier census (acres82) is known for every county and is much more strongly related to acres92 than the region is. Section 4.10 shows how much this matters.

Stratified sampling also has limitations:

It requires information before sampling. We need the stratum membership of every unit and the stratum sizes \(N_h\). For optimal allocation we also need rough values of \(S_h\).
One survey usually measures many variables. A stratification variable that works well for one \(y\) may work poorly for another. A variable highly correlated with one outcome may be nearly uncorrelated with another outcome measured in the same survey. Proportional allocation is a safe compromise, since it never does materially worse than SRS for any variable. An allocation that is optimal for one variable can be inefficient for others.
