title: 5  Ratio and Regression Estimation
text:
5.1 Introduction
When auxiliary information (a variable \(x\)) is highly correlated with our target variable of interest (\(y\)), we can use ratio or regression estimation to improve precision without increasing the sample size. We can also use auxiliary population structures to adjust our estimates after the fact via post-stratification, or estimate means for specific sub-populations (domains).
Throughout, \((x_i, y_i)\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), is an SRS of size \(n\) from a population of \(N\) units, and \(\bar x_U\) (equivalently \(t_x = N\bar x_U\)) is known. Each topic below has the same layout: a theory part that states the estimator, explains where it comes from and gives its standard error, followed by worked examples with data.
The topics are less separate than they look. The ratio, regression and post-stratified estimators each fill in a prediction \(\hat y_i\) for every unit of the population and average them; they differ only in the auxiliary information used to form \(\hat y_i\), and a domain mean is itself a ratio estimator. The regression and post-stratification sections make this explicit, and the post-stratification section ends with a table that puts the estimators side by side.

title: 5  Ratio and Regression Estimation
section: 5.2 Functions and packages for Analyzing Data
text:
5.2 Functions and packages for Analyzing Data
We begin by loading the necessary libraries, including gt for formatting mathematical tables, and defining our custom functions for Ratio, Regression, Domain, and Post-stratified estimation. We also define a versatile gt helper to render our estimation outputs cleanly.

5.2.1 General functions for ratio and regression estimation
The estimating functions used throughout this book (including reg_est, ratio_est, domain_est, srs_est, and the format_est_gt table-formatting helper used below) live in a single shared file, samplingestimate.r, which we source below.
For post-stratification, we reuse the shared str_est() stratified estimator, but we plug in the expected sample sizes \(n_h = n \times \frac{N_h}{N}\) instead of the actual observed random \(n_h\).
The full source of samplingestimate.r is listed in Appendix C.

title: 5  Ratio and Regression Estimation
text:
5.3 Ratio Estimation

5.3.1 Theory

5.3.1.1 The ratio estimator
For ratio estimation to apply, two quantities \(y_i\) and \(x_i\) must be measured on each sample unit; \(x_i\) is often called an auxiliary variable or subsidiary variable. In the population of size \(N\), \[
t_y = \sum_{i=1}^N y_i, \qquad t_x = \sum_{i=1}^N x_i,
\] and their ratio is \[
B = \frac{t_y}{t_x} = \frac{\bar y_U}{\bar x_U}, \qquad \text{so that} \qquad \bar y_U = B\cdot\bar x_U .
\] Ratio and regression estimation both take advantage of the correlation of \(x\) and \(y\) in the population; the higher the correlation, the better they work.
If an SRS is taken, natural estimators for \(B\), \(t_y\) and \(\bar y_U\) are \[
\boxed{\hat B = \frac{\bar y}{\bar x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i} = \frac{\hat t_y}{\hat t_x},
\qquad
\hat t_{yr} = \hat B\, t_x = N\,\hat{\bar y}_r,
\qquad
\hat{\bar y}_r = \hat B\, \bar x_U},
\] where \(t_x\) and \(\bar x_U\) are assumed known. This is the key requirement for ratio estimation: we need to know the population total or mean of the auxiliary variable \(x\) in advance. The ratio estimator is slightly biased, but the bias is negligible when \(n\) is large.
There is a useful way to read these formulas. Once \(\hat B\) is estimated, form the fitted value \(\hat y_i = \hat B x_i\) for every unit in the population, using its known \(x_i\). Summing or averaging these over the population recovers the ratio estimators: \[
\hat t_{yr} = \sum_{i=1}^N \hat y_i = \hat B\, t_x ,
\qquad
\hat{\bar y}_r = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \hat y_i = \hat B\, \bar x_U .
\]
Figure 5.1 shows this for a small population. The grey points are the population, whose \(x_i\) are known, and the green circles are an ordinary SRS. The red line \(\hat y = \hat B x\) is fitted from the sample, and the red points are the fitted values for every unit.


Code
plot_ratio_concept()








Figure 5.1: Illustration of the benefits of ratio estimation. Grey: the population. Green circles: an SRS. Red: the line fitted from the sample and the fitted values for every unit.





This sample happens to have \(\bar x > \bar x_U\), so the naive \(\bar y\) (green) lands well above \(\bar y_U\). The ratio estimator corrects for that through the known \(\bar x_U\): it is the height of the red line at \(x = \bar x_U\), so \(\hat{\bar y}_r\) (red) is close to \(\bar y_U\) (black). Averaged over samples both are (essentially) unbiased, but \(\hat{\bar y}_r\) varies far less.


5.3.1.2 Where ratio estimation is used
Ordinary SRS estimation of a mean or proportion is a special case of ratio estimation, obtained by setting \(x_i = 1\) for every unit: then \(\bar x_U = \bar x = 1\), \(t_x = N\), \(B = \bar y_U\) and \(\hat B = \bar y\), so \(\hat{\bar y}_r = \bar y\) (including \(\hat p\)) and \(\hat t_{yr} = N\bar y\).
Genuine ratio estimation needs an \(x\) whose population total is known more easily than that of \(y\). Three typical situations:

Counting people. Let \(x_i\) be the number of registered births in commune \(i\) of France and \(y_i\) the number of residents. The total number of births is known from administrative records, so \(\hat B = \hat t_y/\hat t_x\) estimates residents per birth, and \(\hat t_{yr} = \hat B\,t_x\) estimates the population of France. For example, if a sample of communes has \(\hat t_y = 2{,}037{,}615\) residents and \(\hat t_x = 71{,}866\) births, then \(\hat B = 2{,}037{,}615/71{,}866 = 28.35\) residents per birth, and with \(t_x = 1\) million births in all of France, \(\hat t_{yr} = 28.35 \times 1\text{ million} = 28.35\) million residents.
Field yield. Let \(y_i\) be the bushels of grain harvested in field \(i\) and \(x_i\) its acreage. Then \(B\) is the average yield in bushels per acre, \(\bar y_U\) the average yield per field and \(t_y\) the total yield. The total acreage \(t_x\) is usually easy to obtain from other records, even when \(t_y\) is not.
The same quantity at an earlier time. When the same quantity is measured at different times, an earlier measurement often makes an excellent auxiliary variable. If the 1987 acreage of every county is known but 1992 acreage is observed only for a sample of counties, let \(y_i\) be the 1992 farm acreage and \(x_i\) the 1987 farm acreage. This is the example used in the simulation study at the end of this chapter.



5.3.1.3 Standard error of the ratio estimator
In large samples the bias of \(\hat{\bar y}_r\) is negligible relative to its variance, so \(\text{MSE}(\hat{\bar y}_r) \approx V(\hat{\bar y}_r)\). To understand the variance, look at the estimation error, \[
\hat{\bar y}_r - \bar y_U = \frac{\bar y}{\bar x}\bar x_U - B\bar x_U = \frac{\bar x_U}{\bar x}\left(\bar y - B\bar x\right),
\] where the second form comes from factoring out \(\bar x_U/\bar x\). Define the population residual of each element as its deviation from the true population line, \[
d_i = y_i - B x_i \qquad (B = t_y/t_x).
\] Then \(\bar y - B\bar x\) is simply the sample mean \(\bar d\) of these residuals, so the error of the estimator is the scaled sample mean of the residuals. Squaring and taking expectations, \[
\text{MSE}(\hat{\bar y}_r) \approx \left(\frac{\bar x_U}{\bar x}\right)^2 V(\bar d),
\qquad
V(\bar d) = \left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac{S_d^2}{n},
\] because the \(d_i\) are fixed population values, so \(\bar d\) is an ordinary sample mean under SRS.
In practice \(B\) is unknown, so the \(d_i\) cannot be computed. We replace \(B\) by \(\hat B\) and use the sample residuals from the fitted line, \[
e_i = y_i - \hat B x_i, \qquad s_e^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 .
\] Substituting \(s_e^2\) for the unknown \(S_d^2\) gives the variance estimators \[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\hat V(\hat B) &= \frac{1}{\bar x^2}\left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac{s_e^2}{n}, \\
\hat V(\hat{\bar y}_r) &= \bar x_U^2\,\hat V(\hat B) = \left(\frac{\bar x_U}{\bar x}\right)^2\left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac{s_e^2}{n}, \\
\hat V(\hat t_{yr}) &= N^2\,\hat V(\hat{\bar y}_r)
\end{aligned}}
\] For samples that are large enough (typically \(n > 30\)) the sampling distributions are approximately normal, and approximate 95% intervals are \(\hat B \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\,\text{SE}(\hat B)\) for the ratio, and the same form for the mean and the total.
The sample residual \(e_i\) is the vertical distance from the point \((x_i, y_i)\) to the fitted line through the origin, \(y = \hat B x\). No centring appears in \(s_e^2\) because \(\hat B = \bar y/\bar x\) forces \(\sum_i e_i = \sum_i y_i - \hat B\sum_i x_i = 0\) exactly, so the residuals already average to zero; the divisor is \(n-1\) for the one parameter \(\hat B\) estimated from the sample. Compare the variance with the SRS one, \(\left(1-\frac nN\right)s_y^2/n\): ratio estimation replaces the scatter of \(y\) about \(\bar y\) by the scatter about the line. That is the whole source of the gain, and the whole risk, since an \(x\) that predicts \(y\) poorly gives \(s_e^2 > s_y^2\) and a less precise estimate than the plain sample mean.


5.3.1.4 When does ratio estimation help?
Let \(R\) be the population Pearson correlation of \(x\) and \(y\), \[
R = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \bar x_U)(y_i - \bar y_U)}{(N-1)S_xS_y}.
\] Comparing \(\text{MSE}(\hat{\bar y}_r)\) with \(\text{MSE}(\bar y) = \left(1 - \frac nN\right)S_y^2/n\) shows that \[
\text{MSE}(\hat{\bar y}_r) \le \text{MSE}(\bar y)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
R \ge \frac{B S_x}{2 S_y} = \frac{\text{CV}(x)}{2\,\text{CV}(y)} .
\] If the coefficients of variation of \(x\) and \(y\) are roughly equal, ratio estimation pays off whenever the correlation between \(x\) and \(y\) exceeds \(1/2\).
The gain can be summarized, analogously to \(R^2\) for stratification, by \[
\frac{\text{MSE}(\hat{\bar y}_r)}{\text{MSE}(\bar y)} \approx \frac{S_d^2}{S_y^2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
1 - \frac{S_d^2}{S_y^2}\ \text{is the proportion of variance removed.}
\] This is not exactly the \(R^2\) of fitting the linear model \(y = Bx\), because \(\hat B\) is not a least-squares estimate of \(B\), but it carries similar information about how much variance ratio estimation removes.

title: 5  Ratio and Regression Estimation
text:
5.4 Regression Estimation

5.4.1 Theory

5.4.1.1 The linear model and the least-squares fit
Ratio estimation works best if the data are well fit by a straight line through the origin, with spread growing with \(x\). Sometimes data instead appear evenly scattered about a straight line that does not go through the origin, so that the usual straight-line regression model applies, \[
y = B_0 + B_1 x .
\] In ratio estimation \(y_i = Bx_i + d_i\) with residual spread growing with \(x\); in regression estimation \(y_i = B_0 + B_1x_i + d_i\) with roughly constant spread.








Figure 5.6: Data suited to ratio estimation (left: a line through the origin, with spread growing with \(x\)) and to regression estimation (right: a line with a non-zero intercept and constant spread).





The ordinary least squares slope and intercept, from the sample, are \[
\hat B_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)^2} = \frac{r\,s_y}{s_x},
\qquad
\hat B_0 = \bar y - \hat B_1\bar x ,
\] where \(r\) is the sample Pearson correlation coefficient of \(x\) and \(y\).


5.4.1.2 The regression estimator
Assuming \(\bar x_U\) (or \(t_x\)) is known, the regression estimator of the mean is the fitted line evaluated at \(\bar x_U\): \[
\boxed{\hat{\bar y}_{reg} = \hat B_0 + \hat B_1\bar x_U = \bar y + \hat B_1\left(\bar x_U - \bar x\right),
\qquad
\hat t_{reg} = N\hat{\bar y}_{reg} = N\hat B_0 + \hat B_1 t_x}.
\] Equivalently, averaging the fitted value \(\hat y_i = \hat B_0 + \hat B_1 x_i\) over every population unit gives the same estimator, \[
\hat{\bar y}_{reg} = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\left(\hat B_0 + \hat B_1 x_i\right) = \hat B_0 + \hat B_1\bar x_U .
\] This is a natural generalization of the ratio estimator \(\hat{\bar y}_r = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\hat B x_i\).
Figure 5.7 illustrates it. The grey points are the population and the green circles an ordinary SRS. The red line is fitted from the sample, \(\hat y_i = \hat B_0 + \hat B_1x_i\) for every unit, and the regression estimate is the average of the red points.


Code
plot_reg_concept()








Figure 5.7: Illustration of the benefits of regression estimation. Grey: the population. Green circles: an SRS. Red: the line fitted from the sample and the fitted values for every unit.





The sampled \(x\)’s average above \(\bar x_U\), so the naive \(\bar y\) (green) sits above \(\bar y_U\); the regression estimator shifts the fit back to \(\bar x_U\) and lands on target, \(\hat{\bar y}_{reg}\) (red) \(\approx \bar y_U\) (black). Both are essentially unbiased over repeated samples, but \(\hat{\bar y}_{reg}\) is much less variable.


5.4.1.3 Standard error of the regression estimator
Let \(e_i = y_i - (\hat B_0 + \hat B_1 x_i)\) be the regression residuals. The estimated variance uses the residual mean square of the regression, \[
\boxed{\hat V(\hat{\bar y}_{reg}) = \left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac{s_e^2}{n},
\qquad
s_e^2 = \frac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(y_i - \hat B_0 - \hat B_1 x_i\right)^2},
\] with \(\hat V(\hat t_{reg}) = N^2\hat V(\hat{\bar y}_{reg})\) and 95% intervals using \(t_{0.975,\,n-2}\). Since \(s_e^2 = s_y^2(1 - r^2)(n-1)/(n-2)\), the standard error is approximately \[
\text{SE}(\hat{\bar y}_{reg}) \approx \sqrt{\left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac1n\, s_y^2\left(1 - r^2\right)},
\] so the stronger the linear relationship, the smaller the SE.
The divisor is now \(n - 2\), since both \(\hat B_0\) and \(\hat B_1\) are estimated. For the same data \(\sum_i e_i^2\) can only be smaller here than under the ratio fit (the ratio line is the special case \(\hat B_0 = 0\)), so the regression estimator is the safer of the two whenever the relationship misses the origin, at the cost of one degree of freedom. Note also that the factor \((\bar x_U/\bar x)^2\) is absent: the fitted line is evaluated at \(\bar x_U\) directly, so no correction for \(\bar x \neq \bar x_U\) is needed.

title: 5  Ratio and Regression Estimation
text:
5.5 Post-stratification

5.5.1 Theory

5.5.1.1 The post-stratified estimator
Sometimes a unit’s stratum is unknown until after sampling, for instance a person’s gender before the interview. We cannot then stratify in advance, but if the true population sizes \(N_h\) of the \(H\) groups are known from another source, we can still take an SRS, sort the units into groups afterwards, and weight each group mean by its known population share \(\pi_h = N_h/N\), as in stratified sampling: \[
\boxed{\bar y_{post} = \sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h\,\bar y_h,
\qquad
\hat t_{post} = N\bar y_{post}}.
\] Compare this with the unweighted mean \(\bar y = \sum_h (n_h/n)\,\bar y_h\), which weights the groups by the shares the sample happened to deliver. When the sample over- or under-represents a group, post-stratification corrects for it.
It also has a predictive reading, like the ratio and regression estimators. Every unit in group \(h\) is predicted by that group’s sample mean, \(\hat y_i = \bar y_h\) for \(i \in \mathcal U_h\), so \[
\hat t_{post} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal U}\hat y_i = \sum_{h=1}^H N_h\,\bar y_h,
\qquad
\hat{\bar y}_{post} = \sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h\,\bar y_h .
\]
Figure 5.10 illustrates the benefit. The grey points are the population, split into post-strata A to D (the width of each block is \(N_h\)). The green circles are an ordinary SRS of \(n = 25\); the realized \(n_h = (5, 5, 6, 9)\) do not match the population shares \(\pi_h = (.36, .14, .21, .29)\), and they never do, since \(n_h\) is random. The red segments are the predictions \(\hat y_i = \bar y_h\) in each stratum, whose weighted average is \(\hat{\bar y}_{post}\).


Code
plot_poststrat_concept()








Figure 5.10: Illustration of the benefits of post-stratification.





This sample is light on A and heavy on D, so the naive \(\bar y\) (green) is pulled up; reweighting by the known \(\pi_h\) undoes it, and \(\hat{\bar y}_{post}\) (red) is close to \(\bar y_U\) (black). It is this reweighting, repeated over samples, that cuts the variance.


5.5.1.2 Variance of the post-stratified mean
The observed group sizes \(n_h\) are random, so for the variance we substitute their expected values under SRS, the proportional sample sizes \[
n_h^{post} = n\,\frac{N_h}{N} = n\pi_h ,
\] into the stratified variance formula. Every group then has sampling fraction \(n_h^{post}/N_h = n/N\), so the finite population correction is the same in all groups and the variance simplifies: \[
\boxed{\hat V(\bar y_{post}) = \sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h^2\left(1 - \frac{n_h^{post}}{N_h}\right)\frac{s_h^2}{n_h^{post}}
= \left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac1n\sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h s_h^2},
\] the variance of proportional stratified sampling: the SRS variance with \(s^2\) replaced by the weighted average of the within-group variances. Also \(\hat V(\hat t_{post}) = N^2\hat V(\bar y_{post})\). Here \(n_h\), \(\bar y_h\) and \(s_h^2\) are the count, mean and variance of the units the sample happened to place in group \(h\), so every group needs \(n_h \geq 2\) for \(s_h^2\) to exist. Substituting \(n_h^{post}\) treats the \(n_h\) as fixed at \(n\pi_h\); carrying their randomness adds a second-order term \(\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_h(1 - \pi_h)s_h^2\), negligible unless some \(n_h\) are small.


5.5.1.3 Post-stratification as a regression estimator
Post-stratification is not a separate technique: it is the regression estimator of Section 5.4.1 with the group indicators as the auxiliary variables. Take the \(H\) dummies \(x_{ih} = \mathbf 1\{i \in \text{group } h\}\) and fit without an intercept. Then

the fitted coefficients are the group means, \(\hat B_h = \bar y_h\);
the population means of those dummies are the known weights, \(\bar x_{U,h} = N_h/N = \pi_h\);

so the regression estimator is the post-stratified one, \[
\hat{\bar y}_{reg} = \sum_h \hat B_h\,\bar x_{U,h} = \sum_h \pi_h\bar y_h = \hat{\bar y}_{post} .
\] Its residuals are each unit’s deviation from its own group mean, \(e_i = y_i - \bar y_{h(i)}\), and the regression variance \(\left(1 - \frac nN\right)s_e^2/n\) applies with \(p = H\) fitted parameters: \[
s_e^2 = \frac{1}{n-H}\sum_h\sum_{i \in h}\left(y_i - \bar y_h\right)^2 = \sum_h \frac{n_h - 1}{n-H}\,s_h^2 .
\] Dropping the \(-1\) and the \(-H\) (small relative to \(n_h\) and \(n\)), and then using \(n_h/n \approx \pi_h\), the regression variance reduces to the post-stratified one: \[
\begin{aligned}
\hat V(\hat{\bar y}_{reg})
&= \left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac1n\sum_{h=1}^H \frac{n_h - 1}{n-H}\,s_h^2 \\
&\approx \left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac1n\sum_{h=1}^H \frac{n_h}{n}\,s_h^2 \\
&\approx \left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac1n\sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h\,s_h^2
= \hat V(\hat{\bar y}_{post}) .
\end{aligned}
\] Both are weighted averages of the same \(s_h^2\); only the weights differ, \[
\underbrace{\frac{n_h - 1}{n - H}}_{\text{sample proportions}}
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
\underbrace{\pi_h = \frac{N_h}{N}}_{\text{population proportions}} .
\] So the substitution \(n_h \to n\pi_h\) above is simply: pool the residuals with the weights we know, not with the ones the sample happened to deliver. It is the same reasoning that puts \(\bar x_U\), rather than \(\bar x\), in the ratio estimator.
Seen this way, the estimators of this chapter are one estimator with different auxiliary variables, and \(s_e^2 = \frac{1}{n-p}\sum_i e_i^2\) throughout, where \(p\) is the number of fitted parameters:









Estimator
Auxiliary variables
Residual \(e_i\)
\(p\)

Domain estimation, treated next, stands slightly apart: there the divisor is the random \(n_d\) rather than the full \(n\), because only the units falling in the domain carry information about it.

The population is the \(N=3041\) counties with no missing value in acres92, acres87, acres82 or farms92.

title: 5  Ratio and Regression Estimation
text:
5.6 Domain Estimation

5.6.1 Theory

5.6.1.1 Domains
Suppose there are \(D\) domains, subpopulations of interest determined only after sampling, such as men and women. Let \(\mathcal U_d\) be the population units in domain \(d\) and \(\mathcal S_d\) the sampled units in domain \(d\), with \(N_d = |\mathcal U_d|\) and \(n_d = |\mathcal S_d|\). We might want the mean salary for men and for women separately, but we do not know a person’s gender before selecting them, so we cannot stratify by domain in advance. Instead we estimate each domain’s mean or total after sampling, by splitting the sample by domain ID.
The domain sample size \(n_d\) is a random variable: a different SRS would very likely give a different \(n_d\). The domain mean is \[
\bar y_d = \frac{1}{n_d}\sum_{i \in \mathcal S_d} y_i ,
\] which looks like an ordinary sample mean, but the randomness of \(n_d\) is the source of the extra uncertainty.


5.6.1.2 Domain means are ratio estimates
Define \[
x_i = \begin{cases}1 & i \in \mathcal U_d\\ 0 & i \notin \mathcal U_d\end{cases}
\qquad
u_i = y_ix_i = \begin{cases}y_i & i \in \mathcal U_d\\ 0 & i \notin \mathcal U_d\end{cases}
\] Then \(t_x = N_d\), \(\bar x_U = N_d/N\), \(\bar y_{U_d} = t_u/t_x = B\), \(\bar x = n_d/n\), and \[
\bar y_d = \hat B = \frac{\bar u}{\bar x} = \frac{\hat t_u}{\hat t_x} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal S_d} y_i}{n_d} .
\] Domain mean estimation is therefore a special case of ratio estimation, with \(\sum_{i=1}^n u_i/\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) as the ratio. This is exactly why it is a ratio estimator and not a simple mean.


5.6.1.3 Standard error of a domain mean
Applying the formula for \(\hat V(\hat B)\) with \(x_i\) and \(u_i\) as defined above gives \[
\boxed{\hat V(\bar y_d) = \left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac{s_d^2}{n_d},
\qquad
s_d^2 = \frac{1}{n_d - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal S_d}\left(y_i - \bar y_d\right)^2},
\] where \(S_d\) is the set of sampled units in domain \(d\), \(n\) is the overall sample size, \(N\) is the population size, and \(s_d^2\) is the sample variance of the \(y_i\) within domain \(d\). (Exactly, the variance is \(\left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac{n}{n_d^2}\frac{(n_d - 1)s_d^2}{n-1}\), which is approximately the expression above.) Ninety-five percent intervals use \(t_{0.975,\,n_d - 1}\).
This is not the same as naively applying SRS within domain \(d\), as if \(n_d\) were fixed, which would use \(\left(1 - \frac{n_d}{N_d}\right)\) in place of \(\left(1 - \frac nN\right)\). Only the finite population correction differs: the overall rate (correct, since \(n_d\) is random) versus the domain rate (wrong). They agree only when \(n_d/N_d \approx n/N\). The fpc uses the overall sampling fraction \(n/N\) also because the domain’s population size \(N_d\) is usually unknown.


5.6.1.4 Estimating a domain total

If \(N_d\) is known: \(\hat t_{yd} = \bar y_d \times N_d\), with \(\text{SE}(\hat t_{yd}) = \text{SE}(\bar y_d) \times N_d\).
If \(N_d\) is unknown: estimate it first, \(\hat N_d = N\,n_d/n\), and use \(\hat t_{yd} = \bar y_d \times \hat N_d = N\bar u\), with \[
\text{SE}(\hat t_{yd}) = N\,\text{SE}(\bar u) = N\sqrt{\left(1 - \frac nN\right)\frac{s_u^2}{n}} .
\]

title: 5  Ratio and Regression Estimation
text:
5.7 Prediction with Machine-Learning Models
The ratio, regression and post-stratified estimators all fill in a prediction \(\hat y_i\) for every unit of the population and average them. Each assumes a specific form for \(E[y\mid x]\): a line through the origin, a straight line, or a constant within each group. More generally, we can fit any prediction model \(\hat m(\cdot)\) to the sample (a smoother, a regression tree, a random forest, a neural network, …) and predict every population unit: \[
\hat y_i = \hat m(x_i), \quad i = 1, \ldots, N, \qquad
\boxed{\hat{\bar y}_{\text{pred}} = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \hat y_i, \qquad
\hat t_{y,\text{pred}} = \sum_{i=1}^N \hat y_i .}
\] The ratio and regression estimators are the special cases \(\hat m(x) = \hat Bx\) and \(\hat m(x) = \hat B_0 + \hat B_1 x\).
In Figure 5.11 the true relationship is curved. A straight line (blue, dashed) underfits it, but a flexible loess curve (red) fitted to an SRS of 15 units tracks it closely, and the average of its predictions, \(\hat{\bar y}_{\text{ML}}\), lands much closer to \(\bar y_U\) than the sample mean.








Figure 5.11: A prediction estimator with a flexible model. Grey: the population (\(x_i\) known). Green circles: an SRS. Red: a loess curve fitted to the sample and its predictions for every unit; blue dashed: a straight-line fit. Left margin: \(\bar y_U\) (black), the sample mean (green) and the mean of the predictions (red).





Two practical points. Because \(\hat m\) may be nonlinear, the estimator needs the value \(x_i\) of every population unit, not just \(\bar x_U\). And there is usually no simple formula for its standard error, which is then estimated by the bootstrap or by cross-validation of the residuals.

  # ratio estimate (Total)
  sim_rat$B[i] <- mean(y_srs) / mean(x_srs)
  sim_rat$ratio[i] <-  sim_rat$B[i] * txU
}

boxplot(sim_rat[, 1:2], main="Estimator Variance: SRS vs Ratio")
abline(h = tyU, col = "red", lwd=2)

percentage_reduction <- 1 - ratio_sim_var

title: 6  Cluster Sampling
text:
6.1 What Is Cluster Sampling?
Suppose we want to find out how many bicycles are owned by the residents of a community of 10,000 households. We could take an SRS of 400 households. Alternatively, we could divide the community into blocks of about 20 households each, select 20 of the 500 blocks at random, and then interview every household (or a subsample of the households) in each selected block. The second plan is an example of cluster sampling. The blocks are the primary sampling units (psus), or clusters. The households are the secondary sampling units (ssus); often, as here, the ssus are the elements of the population.
Why would we sample clusters rather than elements?
The price is usually precision. Figure 6.1 illustrates a two-stage cluster sample from a synthetic population of \(N = 10\) clusters of different sizes, from \(M_i = 40\) to \(160\) units, sorted by their means. Three clusters are selected by SRS (shaded), and an SRS of \(m_i = 20\) units is taken in each. Only the selected clusters are observed. When the cluster means differ, as here, the estimate depends heavily on which clusters happen to be chosen, and a cluster sample is usually less precise than an SRS of the same number of units.
Figure 6.1: A two-stage cluster sample from a synthetic population of 10 clusters of 40 to 160 units, sorted by their means (dashed lines). Three clusters are selected at random (shaded), and 20 units (red) are subsampled in each; the other clusters are not observed at all.
The material in this chapter corresponds to Sections 5.1–5.3 of Lohr and Chapters 8 and 9 of Scheaffer et al.

title: 6  Cluster Sampling
text:
A sampling frame of the observation units may be difficult, expensive or impossible to construct. We cannot list all the honeybees in a region, or all the customers of a store. A list of the individuals in a city may be obtainable only through a list of housing units, which is time-consuming and expensive to build.
The population may be widely spread out geographically, or may occur in natural clusters such as households or schools. It is then much cheaper to sample clusters than to take an SRS of individuals. To survey nursing-home residents, it is far cheaper to sample nursing homes and interview every resident in them than to take an SRS of residents, which might require travelling to a home to interview just one person.





6.1.1 Cluster sampling versus stratified sampling
Both designs partition the population into groups: every element belongs to exactly one stratum, or to exactly one cluster. The difference is in how the groups are used (Figure 6.2). In stratified sampling we take an SRS from every stratum. In one-stage cluster sampling we take an SRS of clusters and observe every element in the selected clusters; the other clusters are not observed at all.








Figure 6.2: The same population of 12 groups of elements (cells), sampled two ways. Left: stratified sampling takes an SRS of elements (red) from every stratum. Right: one-stage cluster sampling takes an SRS of 3 clusters and observes all their elements.





The two designs therefore call for opposite kinds of groups. Stratification gains precision when each stratum is internally homogeneous, because only the variability within strata enters the variance. Cluster sampling loses precision when the clusters are internally homogeneous, because only a few clusters are seen, and the precision depends mainly on the variability between the cluster means. Ideally, each cluster would be a miniature of the whole population.

title: 6  Cluster Sampling
text:
6.2 Notation for Cluster Sampling

6.2.1 Population quantities
In cluster sampling the population \(\mathcal U\) is the population of \(N\) psus. Note the change from earlier chapters: \(N\) is now the number of psus, not the number of elements. Psu \(i\) contains \(M_i\) ssus, and we write \[
y_{ij} = \text{the measurement on the } j\text{th ssu in the } i\text{th psu},
\qquad j = 1, \ldots, M_i,\quad i = 1, \ldots, N .
\] Figure 6.3 displays the population as a row of clusters. Each cluster is a column of cells, one cell per ssu, holding its value \(y_{ij}\). The clusters have different numbers of cells: the size \(M_i\) of each cluster is written at its bottom, and its total \(t_i\) at its top.








Figure 6.3: The population in cluster sampling. Cluster (psu) \(i\) is a column of \(M_i\) cells, one per ssu, holding the values \(y_{i1}, \ldots, y_{iM_i}\). Its total \(t_i = \sum_j y_{ij}\) is shown at the top and its size \(M_i\) at the bottom.





The psu-level quantities are the cluster totals and their spread: \[
t_i = \sum_{j=1}^{M_i} y_{ij} \quad(\text{total in psu } i), \qquad
t = \sum_{i=1}^N t_i \quad(\text{population total}),
\] \[
M_0 = \sum_{i=1}^N M_i \quad(\text{number of ssus}),
\] \[
S_t^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N \Big(t_i - \frac tN\Big)^2 \quad(\text{population variance of the psu totals}).
\] The ssu-level quantities describe the individual elements: \[
\bar y_U = \frac{1}{M_0}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^{M_i} y_{ij} = \frac{t}{M_0} \quad(\text{population mean per ssu}),
\qquad
\bar y_{iU} = \frac{t_i}{M_i} \quad(\text{mean in psu } i),
\] \[
S^2 = \frac{1}{M_0-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^{M_i}(y_{ij}-\bar y_U)^2 \quad(\text{population variance}),
\] \[
S_i^2 = \frac{1}{M_i-1}\sum_{j=1}^{M_i}(y_{ij}-\bar y_{iU})^2 \quad(\text{variance within psu } i).
\] Here \(\bar y_U\), the mean per element, is usually the quantity of interest, and \(\bar t_U = t/N\) is the mean per psu.


6.2.2 Sample quantities
The sample is drawn in up to two stages (Figure 6.4). First an SRS \(\mathcal S\) of \(n\) psus is drawn from the \(N\) psus. Then, in each sampled psu \(i\), an SRS \(\mathcal S_i\) of \(m_i\) of its \(M_i\) ssus is drawn. In one-stage cluster sampling every ssu of a sampled psu is observed, \(m_i = M_i\); in two-stage cluster sampling \(m_i < M_i\) for some psus.








Figure 6.4: A two-stage cluster sample. The psus \(2\) and \(i\) are in the sample \(\mathcal S\) (shaded); within each, \(m_i\) of the \(M_i\) ssus are subsampled (red). The psu totals are not observed and must be estimated, giving \(\hat t_i\).





From the subsample in psu \(i\) we compute the sample mean and the estimated psu total, \[
\bar y_i = \frac{1}{m_i}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_i} y_{ij}, \qquad
\hat t_i = \sum_{j\in\mathcal S_i} \frac{M_i}{m_i}y_{ij} = M_i\bar y_i ,
\] and from the \(n\) sampled psus the unbiased estimator of the population total and the sample variance of the estimated psu totals: \[
\hat t_{\text{unb}} = \frac{N}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \hat t_i, \qquad
\bar t = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \hat t_i, \qquad
s_t^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \big(\hat t_i - \bar t\big)^2 .
\] In one-stage sampling \(\hat t_i = t_i\), the true psu total.


6.2.3 Sampling weights
Ssu \(j\) of psu \(i\) is in the sample if psu \(i\) is selected at the first stage and ssu \(j\) is selected at the second, so \[
P(\text{ssu } j \text{ of psu } i \text{ is selected})
= P(\text{psu } i \text{ selected}) \times P(\text{ssu } j \text{ selected} \mid \text{psu } i \text{ selected})
= \frac nN \cdot \frac{m_i}{M_i}.
\] The sampling weight is the reciprocal, \[
w_{ij} = \frac{N}{n}\cdot\frac{M_i}{m_i}, \qquad
\hat t_{\text{unb}} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_i} w_{ij}\,y_{ij} .
\] If the psus are blocks and the ssus are households, household \(j\) in block \(i\) represents \(NM_i/(nm_i)\) households of the population.

title: 6  Cluster Sampling
section: 6.3 One-Stage Cluster Sampling with Equal Cluster Sizes
text:
6.3 One-Stage Cluster Sampling with Equal Cluster Sizes
Consider first the simplest case: every psu has the same number of ssus, \(M_i = M\), and all of them are observed, \(m_i = M\). This is uncommon in household surveys but does occur in agricultural and industrial sampling. Since every ssu in a sampled psu is observed, the psu totals \(t_i\) are known for the sampled psus, and we can ignore the individual elements. The design is simply an SRS of \(n\) psu totals \(\{t_i, i\in\mathcal S\}\) from the \(N\) psu totals, and the SRS results of Section 3.2 apply directly: \[
\hat t = N\bar t = \frac Nn\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} t_i, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat t) = N\sqrt{\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{s_t^2}{n}} .
\] The population has \(NM\) elements, so the mean per element is estimated by \[
\hat{\bar y} = \frac{\hat t}{NM} = \frac{\bar t}{M}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\bar y}) = \frac{1}{M}\sqrt{\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{s_t^2}{n}} = \frac{\mathrm{SE}(\bar t)}{M} .
\]

6.3.1 Example: GPA in a dormitory
A student wants to estimate the average GPA in a dormitory. Instead of listing all the students and taking an SRS, the student notices that the dorm consists of \(N = 100\) suites of \(M = 4\) students each. The student selects \(n = 5\) suites at random and asks every person in them for their GPA:


Code
gpa <- data.frame(
  suite = rep(1:5, each = 4),
  gpa   = c(3.08, 2.60, 3.44, 3.04,  2.36, 3.04, 3.28, 2.68,  2.00, 2.56, 2.52, 1.88,
            3.00, 2.88, 3.44, 3.64,  2.68, 1.92, 3.28, 3.20)
)
ti <- tapply(gpa$gpa, gpa$suite, sum)      # suite totals t_i
matrix(gpa$gpa, nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE,
       dimnames = list(paste("Suite", 1:5), paste("Person", 1:4))) |>
  cbind(`Total t_i` = ti)

The 20 students are not an SRS of students: whole suites are selected together, and students in the same suite tend to have similar GPAs. Treating them as independent observations overstates the information in the sample. The next section makes this precise.

title: 6  Cluster Sampling
text:
6.4 Comparing Cluster Sampling with SRS
How much precision do we lose by sampling clusters instead of elements? For equal-sized clusters the answer comes from the analysis-of-variance decomposition of the population, with the clusters playing the role of groups:








Source
df
Sum of squares




Between psus
\(N-1\)
\(\text{SSB} = \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^M (\bar y_{iU}-\bar y_U)^2\)


Within psus
\(N(M-1)\)
\(\text{SSW} = \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^M (y_{ij}-\bar y_{iU})^2\)


Total, about \(\bar y_U\)
\(NM-1\)
\(\text{SSTO} = \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^M (y_{ij}-\bar y_U)^2 = (NM-1)S^2\)



with mean squares \(\text{MSB} = \text{SSB}/(N-1)\) and \(\text{MSW} = \text{SSW}/(N(M-1))\).
The variance depends on the between-psu variability. Since every psu has size \(M\), \(t_i - \bar t_U = M(\bar y_{iU} - \bar y_U)\), so \[
S_t^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (t_i-\bar t_U)^2 = \frac{M}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N M(\bar y_{iU}-\bar y_U)^2 = M\cdot\text{MSB},
\] and the variance of the estimated total from one-stage cluster sampling is \[
V(\hat t_{\text{cluster}}) = N^2\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{S_t^2}{n} = N^2\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{M\cdot\text{MSB}}{n}.
\] An SRS of the same number \(nM\) of elements, from the \(NM\) elements, would give \[
V(\hat t_{\text{SRS}}) = (NM)^2\Big(1-\frac{nM}{NM}\Big)\frac{S^2}{nM} = N^2\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{M S^2}{n}.
\] The ratio of the two variances is therefore \[
\frac{V(\hat t_{\text{cluster}})}{V(\hat t_{\text{SRS}})} = \frac{\text{MSB}}{S^2}.
\] If \(\text{MSB} > S^2\), that is, if the cluster means vary more than would be expected from randomly formed groups, cluster sampling is less efficient than an SRS of the same number of elements.

6.4.1 Intraclass correlation and adjusted \(R^2\)
Two measures of how similar the elements within a cluster are, compared with elements from different clusters, are the intraclass correlation coefficient \[
\text{ICC} = 1 - \frac{M}{M-1}\cdot\frac{\text{SSW}}{\text{SSTO}},
\] and the adjusted \(R^2\), which also applies to clusters of unequal sizes, \[
R_a^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{MSW}}{S^2}.
\] Both are close to 0 when the clusters are like random groups of elements, and close to 1 when the elements within each cluster are nearly identical. For equal-sized clusters, the variance ratio can be written in terms of \(R_a^2\): \[
\frac{V(\hat t_{\text{cluster}})}{V(\hat t_{\text{SRS}})} = \frac{\text{MSB}}{S^2} = 1 + \frac{N(M-1)}{N-1}R_a^2 \approx 1 + (M-1)R_a^2 .
\] So \((M-1)R_a^2\) is approximately the proportional increase in variance from using cluster sampling instead of an SRS of the same size. Even a small \(R_a^2\) matters when the clusters are large: with \(M = 21\) elements per cluster and \(R_a^2 = 0.05\), the variance doubles.








Figure 6.5: Left: the cluster means differ a lot relative to the spread within the clusters (\(R_a^2\) large), so sampling a few clusters misses most of the population’s variability and cluster sampling loses much precision. Right: the clusters look like random groups (\(R_a^2\) small), and cluster sampling loses little.





This is the mirror image of stratification (Section 4.7). There, a large \(R^2\) between strata reduces the variance, because every stratum is sampled. Here, a large \(R_a^2\) between clusters increases the variance, because most clusters are not sampled.

title: 6  Cluster Sampling
section: 6.5 One-Stage Cluster Sampling with Unequal Cluster Sizes
text:
6.5 One-Stage Cluster Sampling with Unequal Cluster Sizes
In most surveys the clusters have different sizes: classes have different numbers of students, and counties different numbers of farms.

6.5.1 The unbiased estimator
The unbiased estimator of the total is computed exactly as before, \[
\hat t_{\text{unb}} = \frac Nn \sum_{i\in\mathcal S} t_i, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat t_{\text{unb}}) = N\sqrt{\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{s_t^2}{n}},
\] and \(\hat t_{\text{unb}}/M_0\) is unbiased for \(\bar y_U\) when \(M_0\) is known. But now the cluster totals \(t_i\) vary for two reasons. A psu with many ssus tends to have a large total simply because it has more elements, quite apart from any differences in the \(y\)-values. When the cluster sizes differ a lot, this inflates \(s_t^2\), and with it the variance of \(\hat t_{\text{unb}}\).


6.5.2 The ratio estimator
Since \(\bar y_U = t/M_0\), and \(t_i\) is usually roughly proportional to \(M_i\), estimating \(\bar y_U\) is a ratio estimation problem (see the ratio chapter) with \(y\)-variable \(t_i\) and auxiliary variable \(x_i = M_i\): \[
\boxed{
\hat{\bar y}_r = \frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} t_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} M_i} = \frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} M_i\bar y_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} M_i} .}
\] It is the total of the sampled elements divided by their number, a weighted average of the cluster means with weights \(M_i\). Its standard error follows from the ratio-estimator formula with \(x_i = M_i\): \[
\boxed{
\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\bar y}_r) = \sqrt{\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{s_e^2}{n\bar M^2}}, \qquad
s_e^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}e_i^2, \qquad e_i = t_i-\hat{\bar y}_r M_i ,}
\] where \(\bar M = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}M_i/n\) is the average size of the sampled clusters. The residuals \(e_i\) measure how far each cluster total lies from the line \(t = \hat{\bar y}_r M\) through the origin (Figure 6.6). They are typically far less variable than the deviations \(t_i - \bar t\) about the horizontal line \(\bar t\), which determine \(s_t^2\) and hence the standard error of the unbiased estimator, because the size-driven part of the variation has been removed. Note that the ratio estimator does not need \(M_0\), the total number of elements in the population.








Figure 6.6: Cluster totals \(t_i\) against cluster sizes \(M_i\). The unbiased estimator’s standard error depends on the spread of the \(t_i\) about their mean \(\bar t\) (blue dashed line), which is large because the sizes vary. The ratio estimator uses the line \(t = \hat{\bar y}_r M\) (red), and its standard error depends only on the residuals about that line (dotted).







6.5.3 A toy example: why the unbiased estimator can be bad
Consider a whimsical population of just \(N = 2\) clusters (kennels) of dogs: kennel A with \(M_A = 30\) dogs and kennel B with \(M_B = 10\) dogs. Every dog has exactly 4 legs, so the mean number of legs per dog is \(\bar y_U = 4\), and \(M_0 = 40\). We take a one-stage cluster sample of \(n = 1\) kennel, each kennel being chosen with probability \(1/2\).
The unbiased estimator. If kennel A is selected, \(t_A = 30\times 4 = 120\), \(\hat t_{\text{unb}} = \frac21(120) = 240\) and \(\hat{\bar y}_{\text{unb}} = 240/40 = 6\). If kennel B is selected, \(t_B = 40\), \(\hat t_{\text{unb}} = 80\) and \(\hat{\bar y}_{\text{unb}} = 80/40 = 2\). So \[
E[\hat{\bar y}_{\text{unb}}] = 6\times\tfrac12 + 2\times\tfrac12 = 4 = \bar y_U ,
\] and the estimator is unbiased. But it is never equal to 4: it is always off by 2, even though every dog has exactly 4 legs. All of its variance comes from the different kennel sizes.
The ratio estimator. If kennel A is selected, \(\hat{\bar y}_r = (30\times 4)/30 = 4\); if kennel B is selected, \(\hat{\bar y}_r = (10\times4)/10 = 4\). Both possible samples give exactly the right answer, and \(V(\hat{\bar y}_r) = 0\). The ratio estimator removes the cluster-size variability that made \(\hat{\bar y}_{\text{unb}}\) so unreliable. This is why ratio estimation, not unbiased estimation, is the standard method for clusters of unequal sizes.


6.5.4 Example: algebra class test scores (algebra.csv)
One-stage cluster samples are common in educational studies, since students are naturally clustered into classes and schools. Consider a population of 187 high school algebra classes in a city. An investigator takes an SRS of \(n = 12\) classes and tests every student in them on their knowledge of functions. The classes are the psus, of different sizes \(M_i\), and the students are the ssus.

title: 6  Cluster Sampling
text:
6.6 Two-Stage Cluster Sampling
Observing every ssu in a sampled psu can be wasteful: if the elements in a cluster are similar, measuring a few of them tells us almost as much as measuring all. In two-stage cluster sampling we

select an SRS \(\mathcal S\) of \(n\) psus from the \(N\) psus, and
select an SRS \(\mathcal S_i\) of \(m_i\) ssus from each selected psu \(i\).

The psu totals are no longer observed and are estimated by \(\hat t_i = M_i\bar y_i\) (Figure 6.4).

6.6.1 The unbiased estimator
The unbiased estimator of the total is \[
\hat t_{\text{unb}} = \frac Nn \sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \hat t_i
= \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_i} w_{ij}y_{ij}, \qquad w_{ij} = \frac{NM_i}{nm_i}.
\] Its variance now has two sources: the variability between psus, from selecting only some of them, and the variability within psus, from subsampling: \[
V(\hat t_{\text{unb}}) = \underbrace{N^2\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{S_t^2}{n}}_{\text{between psus}}
+ \underbrace{\frac Nn \sum_{i=1}^N \Big(1-\frac{m_i}{M_i}\Big)M_i^2\frac{S_i^2}{m_i}}_{\text{within psus}} .
\] The first term is exactly the one-stage variance. The second term is the extra cost of not observing every ssu in each sampled psu; it vanishes when \(m_i = M_i\).


6.6.2 The ratio estimator
As in one-stage sampling, the mean per element is estimated by a ratio estimator, now with the estimated psu totals \(\hat t_i = M_i\bar y_i\): \[
\boxed{
\hat{\bar y}_r = \frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\hat t_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}M_i} = \frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}M_i\bar y_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}M_i} .}
\] Its estimated variance is \[
\hat V(\hat{\bar y}_r) = \frac{1}{\bar M^2}\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{s_e^2}{n}
+ \frac{1}{nN\bar M^2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}M_i^2\Big(1-\frac{m_i}{M_i}\Big)\frac{s_i^2}{m_i},
\qquad e_i = \hat t_i - \hat{\bar y}_r M_i ,
\] where \(s_i^2\) is the sample variance of the \(m_i\) elements measured in psu \(i\).
The two terms have a useful interpretation. Writing \(M = \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}M_i = n\bar M\) for the number of elements in the sampled psus, the variance splits into the variance of a ratio estimate computed over the \(n\) sampled clusters, plus the cluster sampling fraction \(n/N\) times the variance of a stratified sample in which those same clusters are the strata: \[
\hat{V}(\hat{\bar y}_r) =
\underbrace{\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right) \frac{1}{n\bar{M}^2}
  \frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} (\hat{t}_i - \hat{\bar y}_r M_i)^2}{n-1}}_{\textstyle \hat{V}_{\mathrm{ratio}}}
\;+\;
\frac{n}{N}
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S} \left(\frac{M_i}{M}\right)^{2}
  \left(1 - \frac{m_i}{M_i}\right)\frac{s_i^2}{m_i}}_{\textstyle \hat{V}_{\mathrm{str}}} .
\] \(\hat{V}_{\mathrm{ratio}}\) is exactly the ratio-estimate variance for \(\sum \hat{t}_i / \sum M_i\), and \(\hat{V}_{\mathrm{str}}\) is exactly the stratified variance \(\sum_h W_h^2(1 - n_h/N_h)s_h^2/n_h\) with the sampled clusters as strata: stratum sizes \(N_h = M_i\), sample sizes \(n_h = m_i\), and weights \(W_h = M_i/M\). Each term \[\hat{v}_i = \left(\frac{M_i}{M}\right)^{2}\left(1 - \frac{m_i}{M_i}\right)\frac{s_i^2}{m_i}\] is one stratum’s contribution; the working tables below carry them in a \(\hat{v}_i\) column whose Sum is \(\hat{V}_{\mathrm{str}}\).
Why is the second piece there at all? If we could see the true cluster totals \(t_i\), the ratio piece alone would be the whole variance. Subsampling replaces \(t_i\) by the estimate \(\hat{t}_i\), and the between-cluster sum of squares absorbs only the fraction \(1 - n/N\) of the noise that this creates; the stratified piece pays the rest. Three special cases follow straight from the formula:

One-stage sampling (\(m_i = M_i\)): every \(\hat{v}_i = 0\), and only the ratio piece survives, as in Section 6.5.
\(N\) unknown or effectively infinite: \(n/N \to 0\), the stratified piece drops out, and \(s_e^2\) alone does the whole job. In practice the second term is often negligible compared with the first.
A census of clusters (\(n = N\)): the factor \(1 - n/N\) kills the ratio piece and \(n/N = 1\) leaves \(\hat{V}(\hat{\bar y}_r) = \hat{V}_{\mathrm{str}}\) exactly. Drawing every cluster is stratified sampling, and the formula says so.



6.6.3 Example: American coot egg volumes (coots.csv)
The data come from Arnold’s (1991) study of the size and volume of American coot eggs in Minnedosa, Manitoba. The clutches (nests) are the psus and the eggs are the ssus. From each of \(n = 184\) clutches, two eggs were measured; the clutch sizes \(M_i\) are known.

book_table(coots)

6.6.4 Example: farm acreage, with states as clusters (agpop.csv)
Neither example above actually exercises the within-cluster term: algebra is one-stage, and coots has an unknown \(N\). To see it at work we need a population whose clusters we can count. The agpop.csv file provides one: its 3,059 counties (dropping those coded -99) sit inside exactly \(N = 50\) states, so the states are clusters of known number and known sizes \(M_i\).

Drawing the sample
We take a two-stage sample: an SRS of \(n = 10\) states, followed by an SRS of \(m_i \approx 30\%\) of the counties in each selected state.


Code
agpop <- acres_in_thousands(read.csv("data/agpop.csv"))
agpop <- agpop[!is.na(agpop$acres92), ]

## cluster sizes M_i: the number of counties in each state
Mi_all <- table(agpop$state)
agpop$Mi <- as.integer(Mi_all[agpop$state])

set.seed(2026)
states <- sample(names(Mi_all), 10)                 # stage 1: n = 10 clusters
agclus <- do.call(rbind, lapply(states, function(st) {
  rows <- which(agpop$state == st)                  # stage 2: m_i = 0.3 M_i
  agpop[sample(rows, max(1, round(0.30 * length(rows)))), ]
}))

c(clusters = length(states), counties = nrow(agclus))


clusters counties 
      10      184 




Computing the estimate directly
Everything the estimator needs is a cluster-level summary: the known size \(M_i\) of each sampled state, the number of counties actually measured in it (\(m_i\)), their mean \(\bar{y}_i\) and variance \(s_i^2\), and the estimated state total \(\hat{t}_i = M_i \bar{y}_i\).


Code
n  <- length(states)                                            # clusters drawn
N  <- 50                                                        # clusters in all

Mi    <- tapply(agclus$Mi,      agclus$state, function(x) x[1])  # cluster sizes
mi    <- tapply(agclus$acres92, agclus$state, length)            # counties measured
ybari <- tapply(agclus$acres92, agclus$state, mean)              # subsample means
si2   <- tapply(agclus$acres92, agclus$state, var)               # within-cluster vars
thati <- Mi * ybari                                              # estimated totals

clus_summary <- data.frame(Mi, mi, ybari, si2, thati)

clus_summary |>
  gt(rownames_to_stub = TRUE) |>
  cols_label(Mi    = md("$M_i$"),    mi  = md("$m_i$"),
             ybari = md("$\\bar y_i$"), si2 = md("$s_i^2$"),

Its variance has the two pieces from the formula above. The ratio piece measures how the estimated totals scatter about the fitted line \(\hat{\bar{y}}_r M_i\):

## ratio piece: the variance of the ratio estimate over the 10 sampled states
ei  <- thati - ybarr * Mi          # ratio residuals

V_ratio <- (1 - n / N) * se2 / (n * Mbar^2)

1.650481e+08 3.513821e+03 


The stratified piece treats those same 10 states as strata, of sizes \(M_i\) inside the \(M = \sum_i M_i\) counties they contain, and is then scaled by the cluster sampling fraction \(n/N\):


Code
## stratified piece: strata = the sampled states, weights W_i = M_i / M
M     <- sum(Mi)                                  # elements in the 10 states
vi    <- (Mi / M)^2 * (1 - mi / Mi) * si2 / mi    # each stratum's contribution
V_str <- sum(vi)                                  # the stratified variance

c(M = M, n_Mbar = n * Mbar, V_str = V_str, scaled = (n / N) * V_str)

title: 7  Unequal Probability Sampling
text:
7.1 Functions and Packages
Unequal probability sampling (UPS) selects units with different probabilities, usually in proportion to a size variable known for every unit in the population. Large units contribute more to a total, so we give them a larger chance of being selected, and correct for this in the estimator. This chapter builds UPS in three steps, each a special case or an extension of the previous one:
Sampling with replacement (UPSWR) is used throughout, since it makes the variance easy to estimate: we make \(n\) independent draws, and on each draw unit \(i\) is selected with probability \(\psi_i\), where \(\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i=1\). A unit may be selected more than once, and it then appears in the sample once per draw. Sampling without replacement is briefly discussed at the end (Section 7.5).
The estimating functions used throughout this book (in this chapter upswr_est and upswr_total for sampling with replacement, upswo_est for sampling without replacement, srs_est, ratio_est and reg_est for comparison, and the format_est_gt table-formatting helper) live in a single shared file, samplingestimate.r, which we source below.
The full source of samplingestimate.r is listed in Appendix C.

title: 7  Unequal Probability Sampling
text:
7.2 The Hansen–Hurwitz Estimator

7.2.1 Theory
The population has \(N\) units. Unit \(i\) has a study value \(y_i\), with population total \(t=\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\) and mean \(\bar{y}_U=t/N\), and an auxiliary variable \(x_i>0\) whose total \(t_x=\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\) is known. If \(y_i\) is roughly proportional to \(x_i\) (for example, the number of physicians of a county and its population), we construct the selection probabilities from \(x_i\): \[
\psi_i=\frac{x_i}{t_x}.
\]
The ratio of each unit. Define, for every unit of the population, \[
b_i=\frac{y_i}{x_i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,
\] and let \(B=t/t_x=\bar{y}_U/\bar{x}_U\) be the population ratio. Since \(y_i=x_ib_i\), \(B\) is the mean of the \(b_i\) weighted by \(x_i\), \[
B=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N x_ib_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N x_i},
\] and once \(B\) is known, the mean and the total follow, \[
\bar{y}_U=\bar{x}_U\,B,\qquad t=t_x\,B,\qquad \bar{x}_U=\frac{t_x}{N}.
\] So estimating \(B\) is enough: we build an estimator \(\hat{B}\) and convert it to \(\hat{\bar{y}}=\bar{x}_U\hat{B}\) and \(\hat{t}=t_x\hat{B}\). Everything below, for HH, the ratio estimator and the sample average, is written in terms of the \(b_i\).
The sample \(\mathcal{R}\) and its observations \(b_j^*\). We make \(n\) independent draws with replacement; on each draw, unit \(i\) is selected with probability \(\psi_i=x_i/t_x\). The sample, denoted \(\mathcal{R}\) (not \(\mathcal{S}\)), is the list of the \(n\) draws including repeats: a unit drawn twice appears twice. Let \(b_j^*\) denote the ratio \(b\) of the unit selected on the \(j\)th draw, that is, the \(j\)th observation in \(\mathcal{R}\) (\(j=1,\ldots,n\)). The star reminds us that \(b_j^*\) is indexed by the draw, not by the population unit: \(b_j^*\) is random, while \(b_1,\ldots,b_N\) are fixed numbers.
Sampling distribution of \(b_j^*\). On every draw, \(b_j^*\) equals \(b_i\) exactly when unit \(i\) is selected, so \(b_j^*\) is a discrete random variable with distribution










Unit selected on draw \(j\)
\(1\)
\(2\)
\(\cdots\)
\(N\)




Value of \(b_j^*\)
\(b_1\)
\(b_2\)
\(\cdots\)
\(b_N\)


Probability
\(\psi_1=x_1/t_x\)
\(\psi_2=x_2/t_x\)
\(\cdots\)
\(\psi_N=x_N/t_x\)



(if several units have the same value of \(b_i\), their probabilities add up). Since the draws are made with replacement, the probabilities do not change from draw to draw, and \(b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*\) are independent and identically distributed (iid) with this distribution. Its mean and variance are \[
E(b_j^*)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{x_i}{t_x}\cdot\frac{y_i}{x_i}=\frac{t}{t_x}=B,\qquad
S_{b^*}^2=V(b_j^*)=\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i\,(b_i-B)^2 .
\] A single draw is therefore an unbiased estimate of \(B\), and it is a precise one when the \(b_i\) are nearly the same for all units, that is, when \(y_i\) is nearly proportional to \(x_i\).
Hansen–Hurwitz estimator of \(B\). The HH estimator is the average of the \(n\) observations in \(\mathcal{R}\), the mean of the ratios: \[
\boxed{\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar{b}^*=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n b_j^*} .
\] Being the mean of \(n\) iid copies of \(b_j^*\), it is unbiased, and its variance is that of one draw divided by \(n\): \[
E(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}})=B,\qquad
V(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{S_{b^*}^2}{n}=\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^N w^x_i\,(b_i-B)^2 ,
\qquad w^x_i=\frac{x_i}{\bar{x}_U}=N\psi_i .
\] Here \(w^x_i\) is the size of unit \(i\) relative to the average, so that \(\psi_i=w^x_i/N\), and the variance is a sum of terms involving only \(w^x_i\) and \(b_i-B\). There is no finite population correction, since the draws are independent. For the same reason, the sample variance of the \(b_j^*\) is an unbiased estimate of \(S_{b^*}^2\), which gives \[
\boxed{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{s_{b^*}}{\sqrt{n}}},\qquad
s_{b^*}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n\left(b_j^*-\bar{b}^*\right)^2 .
\]
Mean and total. Multiplying by the known \(\bar{x}_U\) and \(t_x\), the estimator, its standard error and its estimated standard error all scale by the same constant: \[
\boxed{\;
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\bar{y}}_{\mathrm{HH}}&=\bar{x}_U\,\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar{x}_U\,\bar{b}^*,\qquad
&\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\bar{y}}_{\mathrm{HH}})&=\bar{x}_U\,\frac{S_{b^*}}{\sqrt{n}},\qquad
&\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{\bar{y}}_{\mathrm{HH}})&=\bar{x}_U\,\frac{s_{b^*}}{\sqrt{n}},\\[4pt]
\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}}&=t_x\,\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}=t_x\,\bar{b}^*,\qquad
&\mathrm{SE}(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}})&=t_x\,\frac{S_{b^*}}{\sqrt{n}},\qquad
&\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}})&=t_x\,\frac{s_{b^*}}{\sqrt{n}} .
\end{aligned}\;}
\] In the more general notation of unequal probability sampling, \(y_j^*/\psi_j^*=t_x\,b_j^*\) is the estimate of the total from draw \(j\), so \(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n y_j^*/\psi_j^*\). This form works for any \(\psi_i\), not only for \(\psi_i=x_i/t_x\), and is what the function upswr_total computes; for \(\psi_i=x_i/t_x\), the function upswr_est works directly with the ratios \(b_j^*\).
Variance of the mean and total. The variances of \(\hat{\bar{y}}_{\mathrm{HH}}\) and \(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}}\) are \(\bar{x}_U^2\) and \(t_x^2\) times \(V(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}})\). The variance is small when all the ratios \(b_i\) are close to \(B\), that is, when \(y_i\) is nearly proportional to \(x_i\).


7.2.2 Comparison of the HH, Ratio, and Average Estimators of \(B\)
The ratio estimator and the sample average are used with a simple random sample (SRS) \(\mathcal{S}\) of \(n\) units without replacement. Let \(w^x_i=x_i/\bar{x}_U\) be the size of unit \(i\) relative to the average, and \(d_i=y_i-Bx_i=x_i(b_i-B)\) the residuals about the line through the origin \(y=Bx\). Each estimator is also an estimator of \(B\), which is then multiplied by \(\bar{x}_U\) or \(t_x\).

The ratio estimator (Section 5.3.1) estimates \(\bar{y}_U\) by \(\bar{x}_U\,\bar{y}/\bar{x}\). Since \(y_i=x_ib_i\), \[
\hat{B}_r=\frac{\bar{y}}{\bar{x}}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}y_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_i}
=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_i\,b_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_i},
\] the mean of the sampled \(b_i\) weighted by \(x_i\) (weights adding up to one), and \(\hat{\bar{y}}_r=\bar{x}_U\hat{B}_r\), \(\hat{t}_r=t_x\hat{B}_r\).
The sample average \(\bar{y}\) ignores \(x_i\). Since \(y_i=x_ib_i=\bar{x}_U\,w^x_ib_i\), \[
\bar{y}=\bar{x}_U\cdot\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}w^x_i\,b_i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat{B}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\bar{y}}{\bar{x}_U}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}w^x_i\,b_i ,
\] the mean of the sampled \(b_i\) with weights \(w^x_i\) that do not add up to one, and \(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{avg}}=t_x\hat{B}_{\mathrm{avg}}\).

Table 7.1 compares them with the HH estimator \(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n b_j^*\). Their variances follow from the variances of \(\bar{y}\) and \(\hat{\bar{y}}_r\) for SRS divided by \(\bar{x}_U^2\), using \(w^x_ib_i-B=(y_i-\bar{y}_U)/\bar{x}_U\) and \(w^x_i(b_i-B)=d_i/\bar{x}_U\) (the ratio estimator’s variance is the large-\(n\) approximation), and from the HH variance of the theory section.

The ratio estimator and HH use the same ratios and the same centre \(B\), so their terms differ only in one factor: \((w^x_i)^2\) for the ratio estimator, \(w^x_i\) for HH. HH multiplies the term of the ratio estimator by \(1/w^x_i=\bar{x}_U/x_i\). A unit larger than average (\(w^x_i>1\)) is downweighted under HH, and a smaller one is upweighted. The reason is that HH gives equal weights to the draws because the large units are already drawn more often, whereas the ratio estimator must give the large units larger weights \(x_i\) to compensate for the equal chances. UPSWR therefore wins when the large residuals \(d_i\) belong to the large units, that is, when the spread of \(y_i\) about the line grows with \(x_i\), as it does for county acreages. When the spread of \(y_i\) is the same for all \(x_i\) (so that \(b_i-B\propto1/x_i\)), the SRS ratio estimator does better. When \(y_i\) is not related to \(x_i\) at all, all the \(b_i-B\) are large and both estimators can be worse than the plain sample average. The next section illustrates these cases.

title: 7  Unequal Probability Sampling
text:
7.3 One-Stage Cluster Sampling with PPS

7.3.1 Theory
In cluster sampling, the units of the HH estimator are clusters (primary sampling units, psus), and the study value of unit \(i\) is the cluster total \(t_i=\sum_{j=1}^{M_i}y_{ij}\). In a one-stage design, every element (secondary sampling unit, ssu) of a selected cluster is observed, so \(t_i\) is known for the sampled clusters. The auxiliary variable is the cluster size \(M_i\), known for all clusters. So the notation of Section 7.2.1 changes as \[
y_i \to t_i,\qquad x_i\to M_i,\qquad t_x\to M_0=\sum_{i=1}^N M_i,\qquad \bar{x}_U\to\bar{M}_U=\frac{M_0}{N},
\qquad \psi_i=\frac{M_i}{M_0}.
\] The ratio of cluster \(i\) is \[
b_i=\frac{t_i}{M_i}=\bar{y}_i ,
\] the mean per element (ssu-level mean) of cluster \(i\), and \(B=t/M_0\) is the mean per element of the whole population, which we denote also by \(\bar{y}_U\). Let \(b_j^*=\bar{y}_j^*\) be the mean per element of the cluster selected on draw \(j\). Then everything in Section 7.2.1 applies:
\[
\boxed{\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar{b}^*=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \bar{y}_j^*},\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{s_{b^*}}{\sqrt{n}},\qquad
s_{b^*}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n\left(\bar{y}_j^*-\bar{b}^*\right)^2 .
\]
That is, the estimate of the mean per element is the plain average of the means of the sampled clusters: large clusters are selected more often, and each selected cluster is then weighted equally. Multiplying by the known constants gives the estimates of the three quantities of interest, with their estimated SEs multiplied by the same constants:

The estimator is most precise when the cluster means \(\bar{y}_i\) vary little, that is, when \(t_i\) is nearly proportional to \(M_i\). Note that this differs from the ratio estimator \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}t_i/\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}M_i\) of cluster sampling with a simple random sample of clusters: here the cluster sizes have been used at the design stage, so a plain average replaces the ratio.

title: 7  Unequal Probability Sampling
text:
7.4 Two-Stage Cluster Sampling with PPS

7.4.1 Theory
In a two-stage design, we select \(n\) clusters with replacement with probabilities \(\psi_i=M_i/M_0\), and then take a simple random sample of \(m_i\) elements from the \(M_i\) elements of the cluster on every draw. The cluster total \(t_i\) is no longer observed, so we cannot compute the cluster mean \(b_i=t_i/M_i\) of Section 7.3.1. We estimate it from the subsample, \[
\bar{y}_i=\frac{1}{m_i}\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}y_{ij},\qquad \hat{t}_i=M_i\,\bar{y}_i ,
\] where \(\bar{y}_i\) is the mean of the subsample. The one-stage formulas carry over with the subsample mean \(\bar{y}_j^*\) of draw \(j\) in place of the cluster mean \(b_j^*\): \[
\boxed{\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar{y}^*=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \bar{y}_j^*},\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{s_{\bar{y}^*}}{\sqrt{n}},\qquad
s_{\bar{y}^*}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n\left(\bar{y}_j^*-\bar{y}^*\right)^2 ,
\] and the estimates of the mean per element, the mean per cluster and the total are \(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}\), \(\bar{M}_U\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}\) and \(M_0\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HH}}\), with their SEs multiplied by the same constants, as in the table of Section 7.3.1. Equivalently, each draw estimates the total by \(\hat{t}_j^*/\psi_j^*=M_0\,\bar{y}_j^*\).
There are two differences from the one-stage case. First, a cluster that is drawn twice is subsampled independently on each draw, so the two draws give different subsample means \(\bar{y}_j^*\), and both are kept as separate observations. Second, no second-stage formula is needed for the standard error. The \(n\) draws are independent, and the values \(\bar{y}_j^*\) differ between draws for two reasons, the choice of the clusters and the choice of the elements within them. The sample variance \(s_{\bar{y}^*}^2\) of the values \(\bar{y}_j^*\) captures both, so the variance of the two-stage estimator is computed in exactly the same way as that of the one-stage estimator. This is a major simplification compared with two-stage SRS of clusters, where the variance has a between-cluster and a within-cluster piece. Of course, a larger subsample \(m_i\) makes \(\bar{y}_i\) closer to \(t_i/M_i\) and reduces the variance, but it does so through \(s_{\bar{y}^*}^2\).

title: 7  Unequal Probability Sampling
text:
7.5 UPS Without Replacement

7.5.1 Review of UPSWR and the Horvitz–Thompson Estimator
Review of UPSWR in terms of \(\psi_i\). With replacement, each of the \(n\) draws selects unit \(i\) with probability \(\psi_i\), and draw \(j\) gives the unbiased estimate \(y_j^*/\psi_j^*\) of the total \(t\), since \(E(y_j^*/\psi_j^*)=\sum_i\psi_i\,y_i/\psi_i=t\). The HH estimator averages the \(n\) estimates, \[
\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*},\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{s_u}{\sqrt{n}},\qquad
s_u^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n\left(\frac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*}-\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}}\right)^2 ,
\] where the SE is easy because the \(n\) estimates are iid. With \(\psi_i=x_i/t_x\), \(\frac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*}=t_x\,b_j^*\), which gives the estimator \(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HH}}=t_x\bar{b}^*\) of Section 7.2.1. The drawback of UPSWR is that a large unit can be drawn several times, which is wasteful.
Without replacement. Now \(n\) distinct units are selected, and the design is described by the inclusion probabilities \[
\pi_i=P(\text{unit } i\in\mathcal{S}),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^N\pi_i=n ,
\] for a sample of fixed size \(n\). For a size variable \(x_i\), we take \(\pi_i=n\,x_i/t_x\) (inclusion probability proportional to size, \(\pi\)ps), which is \(n\psi_i\) for \(\psi_i=x_i/t_x\). A unit with \(n\,x_i/t_x>1\) is included with certainty, \(\pi_i=1\), and the other probabilities are recomputed from the remaining units.
The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) estimator. Weighting each sampled unit by \(1/\pi_i\) gives \[
\boxed{\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}} .
\] It has the same form as the HH estimator with \(n\psi_i\) replaced by \(\pi_i\) (the two coincide if no unit is drawn twice). It is unbiased. Let \(I_i=1\) if unit \(i\) is in the sample and \(0\) otherwise, so that \(E(I_i)=P(I_i=1)=\pi_i\). Then \(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}}=\sum_{i=1}^N I_i\,y_i/\pi_i\), and \[
E(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}})=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}\,E(I_i)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}\,\pi_i=\sum_{i=1}^N y_i=t .
\] This needs only \(\pi_i>0\) for all units. The estimator of the mean per unit is \(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}}/N\). When the inclusion probabilities are proportional to a size variable \(x_i\), \(\pi_i=n\,x_i/t_x\), the estimator of the ratio \(B=t/t_x\) is, as for UPSWR, the HT total divided by \(t_x\), \[
\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HT}}=\frac{\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}}}{t_x}=\frac{1}{t_x}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}
=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{y_i}{x_i}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}b_i ,
\] the plain average of the ratios \(b_i=y_i/x_i\) of the \(n\) sampled units, with \(\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HT}})=\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}})/t_x\). In cluster sampling, \(y_i=t_i\) and \(x_i=M_i\), so that \(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HT}}=\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}}/M_0\) is the mean per element (Section 7.3.1).
Variances. For a fixed sample size, with the joint inclusion probabilities \(\pi_{ij}=P(i,j\in\mathcal{S})\), \[
V(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N(\pi_i\pi_j-\pi_{ij})
\left(\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}-\frac{y_j}{\pi_j}\right)^2
\qquad\text{(Sen--Yates--Grundy)},
\] which is estimated unbiasedly by summing over the sampled pairs only, each divided by \(\pi_{ij}\): \[
\hat{V}_{\mathrm{SYG}}(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}
\frac{\pi_i\pi_j-\pi_{ij}}{\pi_{ij}}\left(\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}-\frac{y_j}{\pi_j}\right)^2 .
\] The joint probabilities \(\pi_{ij}\) are hard to compute for most sampling methods, so approximations that need only \(\pi_i\) are used:

Hájek’s approximation (for designs with high entropy), obtained by \(\pi_{ij}\approx\pi_i\pi_j\left[1-\frac{(1-\pi_i)(1-\pi_j)}{\sum_k\pi_k(1-\pi_k)}\right]\) in the SYG estimator: \[
\hat{V}_{\mathrm{H}}(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}})=\frac{n}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}(1-\pi_i)
\left(\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}-A\right)^2,\qquad
A=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}(1-\pi_i)\,y_i/\pi_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}(1-\pi_i)} .
\]
With-replacement approximation: treat the sample as \(n\) draws with \(\psi_i=\pi_i/n\) and use the UPSWR formula, \[
\hat{V}_{\mathrm{WR}}(\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}})=\frac{n}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\left(\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}-\frac{\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}}}{n}\right)^2 .
\] It ignores the factors \(1-\pi_i\) that account for sampling without replacement, so it overestimates the variance, the more so the larger the \(\pi_i\).

For the mean per unit, divide the estimate and the SE by \(N\); for the ratio \(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HT}}\), divide by \(t_x\).


7.5.2 Example: Acres of Farmland in Counties (agpop.csv)
We draw a sample of \(n=100\) of the counties of agpop without replacement, with inclusion probabilities \(\pi_i=100\,x_i/t_x\) proportional to the acres in 1987 (\(x_i\)), and estimate the mean acres of farmland in 1992 (\(y_i\)) per county. (The few counties with no farmland in 1987 cannot be selected and are left out.) The sample is drawn by maximum entropy sampling, a fixed-size design with these inclusion probabilities, from the R package sampling; a county with \(100x_i/t_x>1\) would be included with certainty (none is here).


Code
library(sampling)
agpop <- acres_in_thousands(read.csv("data/agpop.csv", na.strings = "-99"))
agpop <- agpop |> filter(!is.na(acres92), !is.na(acres87), acres87 > 0)
N <- nrow(agpop)
n <- 100
tx <- sum(agpop$acres87)
pik <- inclusionprobabilities(agpop$acres87, n)    # pi_i = n x_i / t_x

set.seed(348)
q_me <- UPMEqfromw(UPMEpiktildefrompik(pik), n)    # set-up of the sampling design
s <- which(UPMEsfromq(q_me) == 1)                  # indices of the n sampled counties
y <- agpop$acres92[s]; x <- agpop$acres87[s]; p <- pik[s]


The mean per county, estimated by HT with the two variance estimators (the plain sample mean ignores the inclusion probabilities and is shown for contrast), and the ratio \(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HT}}=\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}}/t_x\), the acres in 1992 per acre in 1987:


Code
est_ht_hajek <- upswo_est(y, p, N, method = "mean", variance = "hajek")
est_ht_wr    <- upswo_est(y, p, N, method = "mean", variance = "wr")
est_B_hajek <- upswo_est(y, p, N, tx, method = "ratio", variance = "hajek")
est_B_wr    <- upswo_est(y, p, N, tx, method = "ratio", variance = "wr")


To judge the variance estimators, we repeat the sampling 2000 times, and compute the standard deviation of the 2000 HT estimates, which is the true standard error of the design, and the average of the estimated standard errors:


Code
R <- 2000
sim <- matrix(0, R, 5, dimnames = list(NULL, c("est", "se_hajek", "se_wr", "cover_hajek", "cover_wr")))
for (i in 1:R) {
  si <- which(UPMEsfromq(q_me) == 1)
  yi <- agpop$acres92[si]
  eh <- upswo_est(yi, pik[si], N, method = "mean", variance = "hajek")
  ew <- upswo_est(yi, pik[si], N, method = "mean", variance = "wr")
  sim[i, ] <- c(eh["Est."], eh["S.E."], ew["S.E."],
                eh["ci.low"] <= mean(agpop$acres92) & mean(agpop$acres92) <= eh["ci.upp"],
                ew["ci.low"] <= mean(agpop$acres92) & mean(agpop$acres92) <= ew["ci.upp"])
}










Figure 7.3: Estimated variances of the HT mean in 2000 repeated samples: Hájek and with-replacement approximations. The red line is the Monte Carlo estimate of the true variance, the variance of the 2000 HT estimates.













Figure 7.4: HT estimates of the mean acres per county in 2000 repeated samples. The red line is the true mean; the coverage rates of the 95% confidence intervals with the Hájek and the with-replacement variance estimates are given in the subtitle.









Table 7.6: Estimates of the mean acres of farmland in 1992 per county from one sample of 100 counties drawn without replacement

Output Note: The true mean is 310.1 thousand acres per county. The plain sample mean, 834.3, is far off because it gives every sampled county the same weight, although the large counties had a larger chance of being selected; the HT estimate 315.8 corrects for that. The Hájek and with-replacement SEs are 1.98 and 2.06. Over the 2000 repeated samples the true standard error of the HT mean is 2.37, and the average estimated SEs are 2.33 for the Hájek approximation and 2.43 for the with-replacement approximation, which is a little too large, as expected. The violin plots show the whole distribution of the two estimated variances, with the true variance (the variance of the 2000 HT estimates) as a red line: both are centred close to it, the with-replacement one slightly above. The HT estimates of the mean are centred at the true mean, as unbiasedness implies. The 95% confidence intervals, estimate \(\pm\) \(t_{n-1}\) SE, cover the true mean in 94.7% of the samples with the Hájek variance and in 95.5% with the with-replacement variance; the latter is a little above the nominal 95% because its variance is too large. The ratio of the total acres in 1992 to that in 1987 is \(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{HT}}=\hat{t}_{\mathrm{HT}}/t_x=0.998\) (SE 0.006, Hájek).

title: 7  Unequal Probability Sampling
section: 7.6 When to Use Unequal Probability Sampling
text:
7.6 When to Use Unequal Probability Sampling






WarningRemark: UPS is risky unless y is tied to the size variable



The gain from unequal probability sampling depends entirely on how close the ratios \(b_i=y_i/x_i\) are to a constant, that is, on \(y_i\) being roughly proportional to the size variable \(x_i\) used for \(\psi_i\) or \(\pi_i\). Then the variance in Table 7.1 is small, as for the county acreages. Otherwise,

the estimate can be much worse than a plain SRS average, as in the second population of Section 7.2.3, where the sales are unrelated to the floor area;
a unit with a small \(x_i\) but a large \(y_i\) gets a very large weight \(1/\psi_i\) (or \(1/\pi_i\)) when it is selected, so the estimates are unstable, and the sample variance of the \(b_j^*\) that estimates the SE tends to be too small, so that the intervals under-cover.

UPS is therefore used mostly when the size is a good proxy of what is measured: selecting the clusters of a multi-stage survey with probabilities proportional to their number of households or students, auditing by the monetary value of the items, or surveying establishments by their employment. When the size is only loosely related to \(y_i\), use simple random or stratified sampling, with a ratio or regression estimator if \(x_i\) is known, which is much safer than using \(x_i\) at the design stage.

This appendix collects the boxed formulas of the chapters, together with the few companion formulas they rely on, sorted by topic. Each topic starts with its notation; the link after each formula leads to the section where it is derived. All designs draw units without replacement unless stated otherwise (UPSWR draws with replacement).
Confidence interval. For any estimator \(\hat\theta\) in this list, an approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval is \[
\boxed{\hat\theta \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,df}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)}
\] with \(df = n-1\) for an SRS (\(n - H\) for \(H\) strata); for large samples \(z_{\alpha/2}\) may replace \(t_{\alpha/2,\,df}\) (Section 3.4).
